Computer vision · Technical article

Image Processing

The operations that turn one image into another: remapping intensities, convolving with kernels, filtering in the frequency domain, reshaping with morphology, enhancing and restoring, warping geometry and building multiscale pyramids. For each one: the definition, the mathematics, working code with its real output, the failure modes, and exercises.

10 sectionsPython · NumPy · OpenCV · scikit-imageCode run, outputs shown48 exercises with solutions69 Vancouver references

Almost every computer vision system begins by changing its input. A camera pipeline demosaics, denoises and tone-maps the sensor data before anyone sees it; a document scanner flattens shading and binarises text; a medical viewer stretches contrast; a neural network resizes and normalises every image it receives. These are image processing operations: functions that take an image and return another image, rather than a label or a measurement. They improve quality for a human viewer, or they make a later analysis step easier, more accurate or cheaper [1,2].

A digital image is a sampled, quantised function: a grey-level image is an array f[y, x] with H rows and W columns, and a colour image adds a channel axis. Throughout this article y indexes rows (downwards) and x indexes columns (to the right), which matches NumPy's img[y, x] indexing [3]. Operations differ mainly in which input pixels each output pixel depends on, and that gives a useful map of the field (Figure 1).

How to use this article

Each section defines its operations precisely, implements the core idea from first principles in NumPy, checks the implementation against OpenCV [4], SciPy [5] or scikit-image [6], and then measures what the operation actually does on a standard test image. Every code block marked ran was executed with Python 3.13.17, NumPy 2.5.3, SciPy 1.18.1, OpenCV 5.0.0, scikit-image 0.26.0 and PyWavelets, and its output is reproduced verbatim underneath. The test images (camera, moon, coins, page, astronaut, chelsea, coffee) ship with scikit-image; all figures were rendered by the same code. Exercises close each section, with solutions behind a click.

Conventions Images are stored as floating point in [0, 1] unless stated otherwise; uint8 images hold integers 0–255. PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) is 10·log10(1/MSE) in decibels for images in [0, 1]; higher is better, and +6 dB halves the RMS error. SSIM (structural similarity) is a perceptually motivated index in [−1, 1] [7]. Frequencies are in cycles per image unless marked otherwise.

§1Point operations

A point operation computes each output pixel from the input pixel at the same position and nothing else: g[y, x] = T(f[y, x]). The transfer function T is the same everywhere, so it can be drawn as a curve from input level r to output level s, and for an 8-bit image it can be stored completely as a 256-entry look-up table (LUT) [1]. Point operations cannot blur, sharpen or move anything; they only re-label grey levels. That makes them cheap, invertible when T is strictly monotonic, and the right first tool for exposure, contrast and binarisation problems.

1.1 Intensity transformations

Four transfer functions cover most practical needs (Figure 2):

  • Negative, s = 1 − r: reverses polarity, useful when dark detail on a bright field is easier to read inverted (e.g. some radiographs).
  • Logarithm, s = c·log(1 + r): expands dark levels and compresses bright ones. It is the standard way to display quantities with a huge dynamic range, such as a Fourier magnitude spectrum (§4) [1].
  • Power law (gamma), s = rγ: γ < 1 brightens mid-tones, γ > 1 darkens them. Display and camera encodings are themselves power laws: the sRGB standard encodes linear light with an exponent of about 1/2.4 plus a short linear toe, so pixel values in ordinary image files are not proportional to light [8,9]. Arithmetic that models physics, such as averaging, blurring or illumination correction, is strictly correct only after linearising.
  • Piecewise-linear contrast stretch: map an input interval [a, b] linearly onto [0, 1] and clip outside it. Choosing a and b as low and high percentiles (2% and 98% below) makes the stretch robust to a few saturated pixels.

point_ops.pyintensity transforms, Otsu from scratch, adaptive thresholds, dtype pitfalls ran

"""Point operations: each output pixel depends only on the input pixel at the same place."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from skimage import data, filters, util


def gamma(img, g):
    """Power-law transform s = r**g on an image scaled to [0, 1]."""
    return util.img_as_float(img) ** g


def log_transform(img):
    """s = c * log(1 + r), with c chosen so that the maximum maps to 1."""
    r = util.img_as_float(img)
    return np.log1p(r) / np.log1p(r.max())


def stretch(img, p_lo=2, p_hi=98):
    """Linear contrast stretch: map the p_lo..p_hi percentiles to 0..1 and clip."""
    r = util.img_as_float(img)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(r, (p_lo, p_hi))
    return np.clip((r - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1)


def otsu(img):
    """Otsu's threshold for a uint8 image: maximise the between-class variance."""
    hist = np.bincount(img.ravel(), minlength=256).astype(np.float64)
    p = hist / hist.sum()
    omega = np.cumsum(p)                     # class-0 probability for threshold t
    mu = np.cumsum(p * np.arange(256))       # class-0 first moment
    mu_t = mu[-1]
    with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
        sigma_b2 = (mu_t * omega - mu) ** 2 / (omega * (1 - omega))
    return int(np.nanargmax(sigma_b2))       # pixels <= t are class 0


def lut_gamma_u8(g):
    """A 256-entry look-up table: the fast way to apply any point operation to uint8."""
    return np.clip(255 * (np.arange(256) / 255) ** g + 0.5, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    moon = data.moon()                       # low-contrast uint8 image
    p2, p98 = np.percentile(moon, (2, 98))
    print(f"moon: dtype={moon.dtype}, 2nd-98th percentile=[{p2:.0f}, {p98:.0f}], std={moon.std():.1f}")
    s = stretch(moon)
    print(f"stretched: range=[{s.min():.2f}, {s.max():.2f}], std*255={s.std()*255:.1f}")
    for g in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
        print(f"gamma {g}: mean={gamma(moon, g).mean():.3f}")

    # thresholding
    coins = data.coins()
    t = otsu(coins)
    t_sk = filters.threshold_otsu(coins)
    t_cv, _ = cv2.threshold(coins, 0, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY + cv2.THRESH_OTSU)
    print(f"Otsu threshold: ours={t}  skimage={t_sk}  OpenCV={t_cv:.0f}")
    print(f"foreground fraction at t={t}: {(coins > t).mean():.3f}")

    page = data.page()                       # unevenly lit text
    g_bin = page > filters.threshold_otsu(page)
    a_bin = cv2.adaptiveThreshold(page, 255, cv2.ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C,
                                  cv2.THRESH_BINARY, 35, 10) > 0
    s_bin = page > filters.threshold_sauvola(page, window_size=25)
    for name, b in (("global Otsu", g_bin), ("adaptive Gaussian", a_bin), ("Sauvola", s_bin)):
        print(f"{name:18s}: dark ('ink') fraction={1 - b.mean():.3f}")

    # normalisation and dtype pitfalls
    a = np.full((1, 1), 200, np.uint8)
    b = np.full((1, 1), 100, np.uint8)
    print("uint8 200 + 100: NumPy wraps ->", (a + b).item(), " OpenCV saturates ->", cv2.add(a, b).item())
    x = util.img_as_float(coins)
    z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
    print(f"z-score: mean={z.mean():.2e}, std={z.std():.3f}")
    rgb = util.img_as_float(data.astronaut())
    mean, std = np.array([0.485, 0.456, 0.406]), np.array([0.229, 0.224, 0.225])
    print("ImageNet-normalised channel means:", np.round(((rgb - mean) / std).mean(axis=(0, 1)), 3))

    lut = lut_gamma_u8(0.5)
    y1 = cv2.LUT(moon, lut)
    y2 = np.clip(255 * gamma(moon, 0.5) + 0.5, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
    print("LUT == direct formula:", np.array_equal(y1, y2))
moon: dtype=uint8, 2nd-98th percentile=[78, 129], std=13.3 stretched: range=[0.00, 1.00], std*255=42.3 gamma 0.5: mean=0.661 gamma 1.0: mean=0.440 gamma 2.0: mean=0.196 Otsu threshold: ours=107 skimage=107 OpenCV=107 foreground fraction at t=107: 0.388 global Otsu : dark ('ink') fraction=0.362 adaptive Gaussian : dark ('ink') fraction=0.143 Sauvola : dark ('ink') fraction=0.128 uint8 200 + 100: NumPy wraps -> 44 OpenCV saturates -> 255 z-score: mean=3.44e-16, std=1.000 ImageNet-normalised channel means: [ 0.306 -0.184 -0.123] LUT == direct formula: True

The moon image is a classic low-contrast example: although its extreme values span 0–255 because of a few outliers, 96% of its pixels lie between 78 and 129, a fifth of the available range. The 2–98% stretch maps that interval onto the full range and triples the standard deviation (13.3 to 42.3 grey levels). Gamma then redistributes the tones: γ = 0.5 raises the mean from 0.44 to 0.66.

Try it: point operations on camera

1.2 Thresholding

Thresholding is the point operation g = [f > t]: it turns a grey-level image into a binary mask. The whole problem is choosing t. Otsu's method treats the histogram as two classes separated at t and picks the t that maximises the between-class variance [10]:

σ_B²(t) = ω₀(t) ω₁(t) [μ₀(t) − μ₁(t)]² = [μ_T ω₀(t) − μ(t)]² / (ω₀(t) [1 − ω₀(t)]) ω₀(t) = Σ_{i≤t} p_i μ(t) = Σ_{i≤t} i·p_i μ_T = μ(255)

Because the total variance is fixed, maximising σB² is the same as minimising the weighted within-class variance, and the cumulative sums make an exhaustive search over all 256 thresholds cost O(256). Our 12-line implementation returns t = 107 for coins, identical to scikit-image and OpenCV (Figure 3).

A single global threshold fails as soon as illumination varies across the image, because the same ink can be brighter in one corner than paper in another. Adaptive (local) thresholds compute t(y, x) from a window around each pixel. The simplest is a local mean (or Gaussian-weighted mean) minus a constant, as in OpenCV's adaptiveThreshold. Niblack's rule t = m + k·s uses the local mean m and standard deviation s [11]; Sauvola and Pietikäinen modified it for documents to t = m·[1 + k(s/R − 1)] with R = 128 for 8-bit data, which suppresses spurious "ink" in flat background regions where s is small [12]. On the unevenly lit page image, global Otsu labels 36% of the page as ink, mostly the dark left margin; the two local methods find 13–14% (Figure 4).

1.3 Normalisation and data types

Normalisation rescales intensities to a standard range or distribution. Min–max scaling maps [min, max] to [0, 1] and is sensitive to outliers (the reason the percentile stretch exists). Z-scoring, (f − μ)/σ, gives zero mean and unit variance; neural networks are normally trained on inputs standardised per channel, because centred, similarly scaled inputs condition gradient descent better [13]. The widely used ImageNet statistics (mean 0.485, 0.456, 0.406; std 0.229, 0.224, 0.225 for RGB) are a dataset property, not a law: on astronaut they leave channel means of +0.31, −0.18 and −0.12.

Two data-type facts cause more bugs than any algorithm:

  • Integer arithmetic wraps. NumPy computes uint8 200 + 100 as 44 (modulo 256) while OpenCV's cv2.add saturates to 255. Convert to float before arithmetic, or use saturating functions deliberately.
  • Range conventions differ. skimage.util.img_as_float maps uint8 to [0, 1]; arr.astype(float) keeps [0, 255]. Applying a gamma of 0.5 to the second produces values up to 15.97, which every display clips to white.

Finally, a LUT is the fast path for any point operation on 8-bit data: compute T once for 256 values, then index. The last line of output confirms that cv2.LUT with a precomputed table matches the direct formula exactly.

Exercises · §1
  1. A pixel has normalised value 0.25. What does it become under γ = 0.5 and under γ = 2? Which gamma would you use to reveal detail in the shadows of an under-exposed photograph?
    Show solution

    0.250.5 = 0.5 and 0.252 = 0.0625. A gamma below 1 has slope greater than 1 near zero (the derivative of rγ is γrγ−1, which grows without bound as r → 0 for γ < 1), so it spreads dark levels apart: use γ < 1. The cost is compression of the highlights and amplified shadow noise.

  2. Write the linear stretch that maps the moon percentiles 78 and 129 to 0 and 255 for 8-bit data. What does input 100 become, and what is the contrast gain?
    Show solution

    s = 255(r − 78)/(129 − 78) = 5(r − 78), clipped to [0, 255]. Input 100 maps to 110. The slope, 5, is the contrast gain: a difference of one grey level between neighbouring pixels becomes five. Pixels below 78 or above 129 (4% of the image) are clipped, which is the price of the gain.

  3. A histogram has exactly two spikes of equal height at levels 50 and 200. Compute σB²(t) for t between 50 and 199. Which t does Otsu's method return, and is that a problem?
    Show solution

    For every t in [50, 199], ω₀ = ω₁ = 0.5, μ₀ = 50 and μ₁ = 200, so σB² = 0.25 × 150² = 5625: the objective is flat. An argmax returns the first maximiser, t = 50 in our implementation (pixels ≤ t are class 0). Any t in the interval classifies this image perfectly, but on a new image of the same scene with slight noise, a threshold at the edge of the gap is fragile. Some implementations break ties by taking the middle of the flat region (here about 125), which generalises better.

  4. Evaluate Sauvola's threshold t = m[1 + k(s/R − 1)] with k = 0.2 and R = 128 for a bright flat background window (m = 200, s = 10) and for a dark window containing text (m = 120, s = 60). Explain why the rule does not produce noise in flat regions.
    Show solution

    Background: 200 × [1 + 0.2(10/128 − 1)] = 200 × 0.8156 = 163.1. The window's pixels are around 200 ± 10, all well above 163, so none is labelled ink. Text window: 120 × [1 + 0.2(60/128 − 1)] = 120 × 0.8938 = 107.3, between the dark strokes and the paper. In flat regions s is small, so the threshold drops to about (1 − k)m, safely below the local mean. Niblack's m + k s with negative k instead sits only a fraction of the (tiny) standard deviation below the mean, so noise crosses it.

  5. Show that the Shannon entropy of the grey-level histogram can never increase under a point operation. Does this contradict the fact that histogram equalisation (§6) "spreads out" the histogram?
    Show solution

    A point operation is a deterministic function s = T(r) of the grey level. For any random variable R and function T, H(T(R)) ≤ H(R), with equality iff T is one-to-one on the levels that occur, because merging histogram bins can only lose information. Equalisation spreads the occupied levels across the range (larger gaps, higher variance) but cannot split a bin, and on 8-bit data it often merges several sparse bins: §6 measures the entropy of moon falling from 4.88 to 4.72 bits while its standard deviation grows from 13.3 to 74.0. Spreading the histogram and adding information are different things.

§2Convolution and correlation

Most local operations are linear and shift-invariant (LSI): scaling or adding inputs scales or adds outputs, and shifting the input shifts the output. Every LSI operation on a discrete image is a convolution with some kernel h, the system's impulse response [1,14]. Two closely related sums appear in practice:

correlation: g[y, x] = Σ_i Σ_j h[i, j] · f[y + i, x + j] convolution: g[y, x] = Σ_i Σ_j h[i, j] · f[y − i, x − j] (written g = h ∗ f) (i, j run from −r to r for a (2r+1) × (2r+1) kernel)

Convolution is correlation with the kernel rotated by 180°. For symmetric kernels (box, Gaussian, Laplacian) the two are identical; for asymmetric ones (Sobel, motion blur, learned filters) they differ by that flip. Convolution is the operation with the clean algebra: it is commutative and associative, so h₂ ∗ (h₁ ∗ f) = (h₂ ∗ h₁) ∗ f and cascaded filters can be pre-combined, and it becomes multiplication in the Fourier domain (§4). Yet most libraries implement correlation: OpenCV's filter2D documentation says so explicitly [4], scipy.ndimage.correlate does what it says, and the "convolution" layers of deep-learning frameworks are correlations too [15]. Because a learned kernel can absorb the flip, the distinction only matters when a kernel is specified by hand.

2.1 From first principles

The implementation below loops over the kernel taps rather than over pixels: for each tap it adds a shifted, strided slice of the padded image. That keeps the Python loop at k² iterations and lets NumPy vectorise the rest. It is checked against SciPy and OpenCV, and against scipy.signal.convolve2d for the flipped version.

conv.pycorrelation, convolution, padding modes, stride, separability ran

"""2-D correlation and convolution from first principles, with padding and stride."""
import time
import numpy as np
import cv2
from scipy import ndimage, signal

PAD = {"zero": "constant", "replicate": "edge", "reflect": "symmetric",   # ...cba|abcd|dcb...
       "reflect101": "reflect", "wrap": "wrap"}                           # ...dcb|abcd|cba...


def out_size(n, k, p, s, d=1):
    """Output length for input n, kernel k, padding p per side, stride s, dilation d."""
    return (n + 2 * p - d * (k - 1) - 1) // s + 1


def correlate2d(img, kernel, pad="reflect101", stride=1):
    """Cross-correlation: g[y, x] = sum_ij k[i, j] * f[y*s + i - r, x*s + j - r]."""
    kh, kw = kernel.shape
    ph, pw = kh // 2, kw // 2
    f = np.pad(img.astype(np.float64), ((ph, ph), (pw, pw)), mode=PAD[pad])
    H = out_size(img.shape[0], kh, ph, stride)
    W = out_size(img.shape[1], kw, pw, stride)
    out = np.zeros((H, W))
    for i in range(kh):                  # loop over the (small) kernel, not the image
        for j in range(kw):
            out += kernel[i, j] * f[i:i + stride * H:stride, j:j + stride * W:stride]
    return out


def convolve2d(img, kernel, **kw):
    """Convolution = correlation with the kernel flipped in both axes."""
    return correlate2d(img, kernel[::-1, ::-1], **kw)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    f = rng.random((7, 9))
    k = np.array([[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, -1], [3, 0, 1]], float)     # deliberately asymmetric

    ours_c = correlate2d(f, k)
    print("ours vs scipy.ndimage.correlate:", np.abs(ours_c - ndimage.correlate(f, k, mode="mirror")).max())
    print("ours vs cv2.filter2D          :", np.abs(ours_c - cv2.filter2D(f, -1, k)).max())
    ours_v = convolve2d(f, k, pad="zero")
    print("conv vs scipy.signal.convolve2d:", np.abs(ours_v - signal.convolve2d(f, k, mode="same")).max())
    print("correlation == convolution for this k?", np.allclose(ours_c, convolve2d(f, k)))

    # impulse response: correlation returns the kernel rotated by 180 degrees
    delta = np.zeros((5, 5)); delta[2, 2] = 1
    print("correlate(delta, k)=\n", correlate2d(delta, k, pad="zero")[1:4, 1:4].astype(int))

    row = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])
    for pad in PAD:
        print(f"{pad:10s}", np.pad(row, 2, mode=PAD[pad]),
              " box-3 at left edge:", round(correlate2d(row[None].astype(float), np.ones((1, 3)) / 3, pad=pad)[0, 0], 3))

    for n, kk, p, s in [(224, 3, 1, 1), (224, 3, 1, 2), (224, 7, 3, 2), (5, 3, 0, 2)]:
        print(f"n={n} k={kk} p={p} s={s} -> {out_size(n, kk, p, s)}")
    print("stride-2 shape:", correlate2d(rng.random((224, 224)), np.ones((3, 3)), stride=2).shape)

    # separability: a rank-1 kernel factors into a column times a row
    g1 = cv2.getGaussianKernel(31, 5.0)            # 31x1 column
    G = g1 @ g1.T
    print("rank of 2-D Gaussian:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(G), " rank of Laplacian:",
          np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.array([[0, 1, 0], [1, -4, 1], [0, 1, 0]])))
    img = rng.random((1024, 1024)).astype(np.float32)
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); a = cv2.filter2D(img, -1, G.astype(np.float32)); t1 = time.perf_counter()
    b = cv2.sepFilter2D(img, -1, g1.astype(np.float32), g1.astype(np.float32)); t2 = time.perf_counter()
    print(f"31x31 full: {1e3*(t1-t0):.1f} ms  separable: {1e3*(t2-t1):.1f} ms  max diff {np.abs(a-b).max():.1e}")
    print("multiplies per pixel: full", 31 * 31, " separable", 2 * 31)

False correlate(delta, k)= [[ 1 0 3] [-1 1 0] [ 0 2 1]] zero [0 0 1 2 3 4 0 0] box-3 at left edge: 1.0 replicate [1 1 1 2 3 4 4 4] box-3 at left edge: 1.333 reflect [2 1 1 2 3 4 4 3] box-3 at left edge: 1.333 reflect101 [3 2 1 2 3 4 3 2] box-3 at left edge: 1.667 wrap [3 4 1 2 3 4 1 2] box-3 at left edge: 2.333 n=224 k=3 p=1 s=1 -> 224 n=224 k=3 p=1 s=2 -> 112 n=224 k=7 p=3 s=2 -> 112 n=5 k=3 p=0 s=2 -> 2 stride-2 shape: (112, 112) rank of 2-D Gaussian: 1 rank of Laplacian: 2 31x31 full: 22.6 ms separable: 22.6 ms max diff 2.4e-07 multiplies per pixel: full 961 separable 62

The impulse test shows the flip directly: correlating a single bright pixel with h reproduces h rotated by 180°, which is why convolution, not correlation, has the kernel as its impulse response. For this asymmetric kernel, correlation and convolution give different images.

2.2 Padding

Near the border the kernel reaches outside the image, so a rule must invent the missing values. The output shows the five common rules on the row [1 2 3 4]; their names differ between libraries, which is a frequent source of off-by-one disagreements:

RulePadded rowNumPy np.padOpenCV borderTypical use
zero / constant0 0 | 1 2 3 4 | 0 0constantBORDER_CONSTANTCNNs; darkens borders after blurring
replicate1 1 | 1 2 3 4 | 4 4edgeBORDER_REPLICATEsmooth borders, flat extrapolation
reflect (edge repeated)2 1 | 1 2 3 4 | 4 3symmetricBORDER_REFLECTDCT-like symmetric extension
reflect-101 (edge not repeated)3 2 | 1 2 3 4 | 3 2reflectBORDER_REFLECT_101 (default)OpenCV's default for filtering
wrap (circular)3 4 | 1 2 3 4 | 1 2wrapBORDER_WRAPmatches the DFT's periodicity (§4)

Zero padding biases a smoothing filter towards black at the edges (the 3-tap box gives 1.0 at the left edge instead of a value near 1.3–1.7). Reflection keeps the local statistics plausible, which is why OpenCV makes reflect-101 its default [4]. Circular padding is never visually plausible for natural images, but it is what an FFT-based filter implicitly uses unless the image is padded first.

2.3 Stride and dilation

Stride s evaluates the filter at every s-th position, so it is filtering followed by subsampling. The output-size formula in Figure 5 follows by counting placements of a kernel of effective extent d(k − 1) + 1 in a padded line of length n + 2p [15]. A 7 × 7 stride-2 convolution with padding 3 halves a 224-pixel input to 112, the configuration used in the stem of many CNNs. Dilation d spaces the kernel taps d pixels apart, enlarging the receptive field without extra parameters. Subsampling without enough low-pass filtering aliases (§4, §8): a stride-2 sample of a one-pixel checkerboard is a constant image. Zhang showed that the max-pooling and strided layers of standard CNNs are therefore not shift-invariant, and that inserting a small blur before subsampling restores much of the invariance [16].

Try it: convolution arithmetic

2.4 Separability and cost

A direct k × k filter costs k² multiply–adds per pixel. If the kernel is an outer product of a column and a row (matrix rank 1), the 2-D filter can be applied as a 1-D column pass followed by a 1-D row pass at 2k operations. The Gaussian is separable because exp(−(x² + y²)/2σ²) = exp(−x²/2σ²)·exp(−y²/2σ²); the output confirms that its 31 × 31 kernel has rank 1, cutting the work from 961 to 62 multiplies per pixel. The measured speed-up is smaller than 15× because OpenCV's filter2D switches to an FFT-based algorithm for large kernels. The 4-neighbour Laplacian has rank 2 and is a sum of two separable kernels. A general kernel can be approximated by truncating its singular value decomposition, and box filters cost O(1) per pixel with running sums, a trick that also makes repeated box filtering a fast Gaussian approximation; recursive (IIR) filters achieve the same for the Gaussian directly [17].

Exercises · §2
  1. Compute output sizes for n = 32 with (a) k = 5, p = 0, s = 1; (b) k = 5, p = 2, s = 2; (c) k = 3, d = 2, p = 2, s = 1. Check your answers with out_size or the calculator above.
    Show solution

    (a) ⌊(32 − 4 − 1)/1⌋ + 1 = 28 ("valid"). (b) ⌊(32 + 4 − 4 − 1)/2⌋ + 1 = ⌊31/2⌋ + 1 = 16. (c) The dilated kernel spans 2·2 + 1 = 5 pixels, so ⌊(32 + 4 − 4 − 1)/1⌋ + 1 = 32: padding d(k − 1)/2 = 2 keeps the size.

  2. The horizontal Sobel kernel has rows (−1, 0, 1), (−2, 0, 2), (−1, 0, 1). What is the relation between correlating and convolving an image with it? On a step edge from dark (left) to bright (right), which of the two gives a positive response?
    Show solution

    Rotating this kernel by 180° negates it (it is antisymmetric in x and symmetric in y), so convolution = −correlation. Correlation computes (right neighbours − left neighbours), which is positive on a dark-to-bright edge; convolution gives the negative. Gradient code that silently switches between filter2D (correlation) and scipy.signal.convolve2d therefore flips gradient directions.

  3. Using the padding table, compute by hand the 3-tap box filter at the left end of [1 2 3 4] under replicate and wrap padding, and compare with the program output.
    Show solution

    Replicate: (1 + 1 + 2)/3 = 1.333. Wrap: the left neighbour of 1 is 4, so (4 + 1 + 2)/3 = 2.333. Both match the output. Wrap pulls in a value from the opposite edge of the image, which is why circular boundary effects appear as a bright or dark rim after FFT filtering.

  4. A 3 × 3 box filter applied twice equals one convolution with what kernel? How many multiply–adds per pixel does the separable implementation of that kernel need, compared with the direct 2-D form?
    Show solution

    By associativity, box ∗ box: in 1-D, [1 1 1]/3 ∗ [1 1 1]/3 = [1 2 3 2 1]/9, so the 2-D kernel is the outer product of [1 2 3 2 1]/9 with itself, a 5 × 5 "tent" (already closer to a Gaussian, as the central limit theorem predicts for repeated boxes). Separably it needs 5 + 5 = 10 multiply–adds per pixel versus 25 directly, or 4 additions per pixel with two passes of running-sum box filters.

  5. Take the 1-D signal 1, 0, 1, 0, … (period 2). What does stride-2 subsampling return, starting at index 0 and at index 1? What does a [1 2 1]/4 blur followed by stride 2 return? Relate this to shift invariance in CNNs.
    Show solution

    Without blur: all ones from index 0, all zeros from index 1. A one-pixel shift of the input changes the output completely. With the [1 2 1]/4 blur, every interior sample becomes (1 + 0 + 1)/4 or (0 + 2 + 0)/4, which is 0.5 in both cases, so both phases give the constant 0.5. The blur removes the frequency that stride 2 cannot represent (exactly the Nyquist frequency here), which is the anti-aliasing argument behind blur-pooling [16].

§3Spatial filtering: smoothing and sharpening

Filters are the workhorses of local processing. Smoothing filters suppress noise and fine detail; sharpening filters accentuate edges. The basic tension is that noise and edges are both high-frequency content, so a linear filter that removes one removes the other. The non-linear filters in this section (median, bilateral) exist to break that tie [1,2].

3.1 Linear smoothing: box and Gaussian

The box (mean) filter averages a k × k window. It is the cheapest smoother, but its frequency response is a sinc with negative side lobes, so it lets some fine detail through with inverted contrast and produces blocky artefacts. The Gaussian filter weights neighbours by exp(−(x² + y²)/2σ²). It is the only kernel that is both separable and rotationally symmetric, its Fourier transform is again a Gaussian (no side lobes, no ringing), and cascading Gaussians adds variances: σ² = σ₁² + σ₂² [18]. Those properties make it the default smoother and the basis of scale space (§9).

σ, not the kernel width, defines a Gaussian. The kernel must be wide enough that the truncated tails do not matter: ±3σ contains 99.73% of the 1-D mass. When asked to choose the size itself, OpenCV uses about ±4σ for floating-point images; the program below reads the width off an impulse response and finds 7, 11, 17 and 41 taps for σ = 0.8, 1.2, 2 and 5. For 8-bit images OpenCV's source uses ±3σ instead, and scikit-image's gaussian truncates at 4σ by default.

3.2 Non-linear smoothing: median and bilateral

The median filter replaces each pixel by the median of its window [19]. A median ignores outliers completely as long as fewer than half the window values are corrupted, so it removes impulse ("salt-and-pepper") noise that a mean would merely smear. It also preserves step edges: in a window straddling a clean step, the median is a value from the majority side. Its weaknesses are that it rounds corners, removes thin lines narrower than half the window, and is not linear, so it has no frequency response. Sorting k² values per pixel is expensive; running-histogram algorithms reduce the cost to O(k) [20] and then to O(1) per pixel [21].

The bilateral filter of Tomasi and Manduchi is a weighted mean whose weights fall off with both spatial distance and intensity difference [22]:

g(p) = (1/W_p) Σ_{q∈N(p)} G_σs(‖p − q‖) · G_σr(|f(p) − f(q)|) · f(q) W_p = Σ_q G_σs(‖p − q‖) · G_σr(|f(p) − f(q)|)

Pixels across an edge differ strongly in intensity, so the range weight Gσr excludes them and the edge survives. The filter is not separable and is costly in its direct form; fast approximations work in a downsampled space–intensity grid [23], and the guided filter achieves similar edge-preserving smoothing in O(1) time per pixel with a local linear model [24]. Anisotropic diffusion is the PDE relative of the same idea: diffuse within regions, not across edges [25].

filtering.pyfour smoothers on two noise types, Gaussian kernel size, sharpening ran

"""Smoothing and sharpening filters compared on two kinds of noise."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from skimage import data, util, metrics, filters


def psnr(ref, x):
    return metrics.peak_signal_noise_ratio(ref, np.clip(x, 0, 1), data_range=1.0)


def edge_mask(clean):
    """Pixels within 2 px of a Canny edge of the clean image."""
    e = cv2.Canny((clean * 255).astype(np.uint8), 50, 150)
    return cv2.dilate(e, np.ones((5, 5), np.uint8)) > 0


def psnr_on(ref, x, m):
    mse = np.mean((ref[m] - np.clip(x, 0, 1)[m]) ** 2)
    return 10 * np.log10(1.0 / mse)


def grad_energy(x):
    """Mean Sobel gradient magnitude: a simple sharpness score."""
    gx, gy = cv2.Sobel(x, cv2.CV_64F, 1, 0), cv2.Sobel(x, cv2.CV_64F, 0, 1)
    return np.hypot(gx, gy).mean()


def unsharp(img, sigma=2.0, amount=1.0):
    """Unsharp mask: add back amount * (image - blurred image)."""
    blur = cv2.GaussianBlur(img, (0, 0), sigma)
    return img + amount * (img - blur)


def laplacian_sharpen(img, c=1.0):
    lap = cv2.Laplacian(img, cv2.CV_64F, ksize=1)    # 4-neighbour kernel [[0,1,0],[1,-4,1],[0,1,0]]
    return img - c * lap


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
    clean = util.img_as_float(data.camera())
    gauss = clean + rng.normal(0, 0.08, clean.shape)
    sp = util.random_noise(clean, mode="s&p", amount=0.08, rng=2)

    filters_ = {
        "box 5x5":            lambda x: cv2.blur(x, (5, 5)),
        "Gaussian s=1.2":     lambda x: cv2.GaussianBlur(x, (0, 0), 1.2),
        "median 5x5":         lambda x: cv2.medianBlur(x.astype(np.float32), 5),
        "bilateral 9,0.15,3": lambda x: cv2.bilateralFilter(x.astype(np.float32), 9, 0.15, 3),
    }
    m = edge_mask(clean)
    print(f"edge pixels: {m.mean():.1%} of the image")
    print(f"{'filter':20s} {'PSNR gauss':>10s} {'(edges)':>8s} {'PSNR s&p':>9s} {'(edges)':>8s}")
    rows = [("(noisy input)", gauss, sp)] + [(n, fn(gauss), fn(sp)) for n, fn in filters_.items()]
    for name, a, b in rows:
        print(f"{name:20s} {psnr(clean, a):10.2f} {psnr_on(clean, a, m):8.2f} {psnr(clean, b):9.2f} {psnr_on(clean, b, m):8.2f}")

    # the kernel size OpenCV chooses when you pass ksize=(0, 0): read it off an impulse response
    imp = np.zeros((101, 101), np.float32); imp[50, 50] = 1
    for s in (0.8, 1.2, 2.0, 5.0):
        print(f"sigma={s}: kernel width chosen for float32 input = {(cv2.GaussianBlur(imp, (0, 0), s)[50] > 0).sum()}")

    # sharpening a slightly blurred image
    soft = cv2.GaussianBlur(clean, (0, 0), 1.5)
    for name, x in [("blurred", soft), ("unsharp s=2 a=1", unsharp(soft)), ("unsharp s=2 a=2", unsharp(soft, 2, 2)),
                    ("Laplacian c=1", laplacian_sharpen(soft))]:
        over = (x > 1).mean() + (x < 0).mean()
        print(f"{name:16s} PSNR={psnr(clean, x):6.2f}  sharpness={grad_energy(x)/grad_energy(clean):.2f}x clean  clipped={100*over:.2f}%")
    print("skimage unsharp_mask == ours:", np.allclose(filters.unsharp_mask(soft, radius=2, amount=1, preserve_range=True)[50:-50, 50:-50],
                                                      unsharp(soft)[50:-50, 50:-50], atol=2e-3))
edge pixels: 38.7% of the image filter PSNR gauss (edges) PSNR s&p (edges) (noisy input) 22.26 22.05 15.79 16.36 box 5x5 26.23 22.53 24.24 21.73 Gaussian s=1.2 27.54 24.11 24.60 22.75 median 5x5 26.82 23.39 27.77 23.81 bilateral 9,0.15,3 28.81 26.07 16.07 16.79 sigma=0.8: kernel width chosen for float32 input = 7 sigma=1.2: kernel width chosen for float32 input = 11 sigma=2.0: kernel width chosen for float32 input = 17 sigma=5.0: kernel width chosen for float32 input = 41 blurred PSNR= 27.32 sharpness=0.50x clean clipped=0.00% unsharp s=2 a=1 PSNR= 29.05 sharpness=0.69x clean clipped=0.17% unsharp s=2 a=2 PSNR= 28.74 sharpness=0.91x clean clipped=1.12% Laplacian c=1 PSNR= 29.31 sharpness=0.65x clean clipped=0.03% skimage unsharp_mask == ours: True

The table is the core lesson of this section. With Gaussian noise every smoother helps, and the bilateral filter wins, especially near edges (26.1 dB versus 24.1 dB for the Gaussian within 2 pixels of a Canny edge), because it refuses to average across them. With salt-and-pepper noise the ranking reverses: the median recovers 27.8 dB, the linear filters spread each impulse into a grey blotch, and the bilateral filter barely changes the image (16.1 dB from 15.8 dB). An impulse differs from all its neighbours by far more than σr, so the range weights of the neighbours are almost zero and the pixel is "preserved" as if it were an edge. Choose the filter for the noise model.

3.3 Sharpening

Sharpening adds back an estimate of the high-frequency detail. The unsharp mask, borrowed from darkroom practice, subtracts a blurred copy to get the detail layer and adds a multiple of it:

g = f + a · (f − G_σ ∗ f) frequency response: 1 + a · (1 − Ĝ_σ(ω))

The response is 1 at DC (flat regions are unchanged) and rises to 1 + a at high frequencies. The Laplacian ∇²f = ∂²f/∂x² + ∂²f/∂y², discretised as the kernel with rows (0, 1, 0), (1, −4, 1), (0, 1, 0), gives the related rule g = f − c∇²f [1]. The two are close relatives: for small σ, f − Gσ ∗ f ≈ −(σ²/2)∇²f. Sharpening cannot recover detail that the blur destroyed (that is restoration, §7); it only boosts what is left, including the noise, and it creates halos (overshoot) beside edges. The output measures both effects on an image blurred with σ = 1.5: unsharp masking with a = 2 restores 91% of the original gradient energy but pushes 1.1% of the pixels out of range, and PSNR is lower than with a = 1 because the overshoot is itself an error.

Exercises · §3
  1. A 3 × 3 window contains eight pixels with value 10 except one 255 (salt) and one 0 (pepper), so the values are {10, 10, 10, 10, 255, 10, 10, 0, 10}. Compute the mean and the median. How many corrupted pixels can a 3 × 3 median tolerate in the worst case?
    Show solution

    Sum = 7 × 10 + 255 + 0 = 325, mean = 36.1. Sorted: 0, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 255, so the median is 10, exactly right. The median is correct as long as the 5th order statistic is uncorrupted; in the worst case (all outliers on the same side) up to 4 of the 9 values may be outliers. With mixed salt and pepper some extra margin exists, but 4 is the guarantee.

  2. Why does the bilateral filter leave salt-and-pepper noise almost untouched (16.07 dB versus 15.79 dB input), while doing best on Gaussian noise?
    Show solution

    For an impulse pixel p of value 1 among neighbours near 0.4, |f(p) − f(q)| ≈ 0.6 = 4σr with σr = 0.15, so Gσr ≈ exp(−8) ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁴ for every neighbour, while the centre weight is 1. The output is essentially the impulse itself. Gaussian noise of σ = 0.08 is within σr, so neighbours within a region get substantial weight and are averaged, while pixels across real edges (differences of 0.3–0.8) do not. The range kernel cannot tell an isolated outlier from a tiny one-pixel object.

  3. Show that the unsharp mask has gain 1 at DC and 1 + a at high frequencies. For a = 2, by what factor is white noise at the highest frequencies amplified, and why does this argue for denoising before sharpening?
    Show solution

    The Gaussian's transfer function Ĝσ(ω) = exp(−σ²ω²/2) is 1 at ω = 0 and tends to 0 for large ω. Hence 1 + a(1 − Ĝ) goes from 1 to 1 + a = 3: high-frequency noise amplitude triples (power × 9). Signal detail at those frequencies, already attenuated by the original blur, gains the same factor, so SNR at those frequencies is unchanged while visible noise grows. Denoising first removes noise that sharpening would otherwise amplify.

  4. For a Gaussian blur of σ = 2, which of 9, 13 or 17 taps would you use for a floating-point image, and what fraction of the 2-D kernel mass does a ±3σ square window hold?
    Show solution

    ±3σ needs 2·6 + 1 = 13 taps; ±4σ, OpenCV's choice for float images, gives 17 (as measured), and 9 taps (±2σ) loses 4.6% of the mass per axis. The 1-D mass within ±3σ is 0.9973, so the square window holds 0.9973² = 0.9946 of the 2-D mass; within ±4σ it is 0.99994² ≈ 0.9999. 13 taps are adequate for display; 17 are safer when the result feeds a derivative or a pyramid.

  5. Show that a median filter preserves a perfect step edge (a constant a on the left and b on the right) exactly, but that a 3 × 3 median deletes a one-pixel-wide line. What window shape would preserve horizontal lines?
    Show solution

    At any pixel near the step, the window straddling the edge contains a majority of pixels from the pixel's own side (at least 6 of 9 for a vertical step at the pixel's column, since the window centre column belongs to the pixel's side). The median is that side's value, so the step is preserved. A one-pixel line occupies only 3 of 9 window pixels, a minority, so the median returns the background. A 1 × 5 horizontal window (or a cross-shaped window with a horizontal arm) contains a majority of line pixels along a horizontal line and preserves it; directional medians generalise this.

§4Frequency-domain processing

Any M × N image can be written exactly as a sum of 2-D complex sinusoids. The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) gives their coefficients:

F[v, u] = Σ_{y=0}^{M−1} Σ_{x=0}^{N−1} f[y, x] · exp(−2πi (v·y/M + u·x/N)) f[y, x] = (1/MN) Σ_v Σ_u F[v, u] · exp(+2πi (v·y/M + u·x/N))

Each coefficient is a complex number: its magnitude says how much of the sinusoid with frequency (u, v) cycles per image is present, its phase says where its peaks lie. F[0, 0] is the sum of all pixels (DC), low indices are slow variations, and indices near N/2 are the finest patterns the grid can hold (the Nyquist limit) [1,26]. The fast Fourier transform computes the DFT in O(MN log MN) operations instead of O((MN)²) [27]; NumPy and SciPy call optimised FFT kernels of the same family as FFTW [28].

The reason to leave the pixel domain is the convolution theorem: circular convolution in space is pointwise multiplication of spectra, h ∗ f ↔ H·F. A filter can therefore be designed directly as a transfer function H(u, v) that says which frequencies to keep, and applied with two FFTs and one multiplication (Figure 8). For large kernels this is also faster than direct convolution.

frequency.pyDFT identities, ideal/Butterworth/Gaussian filters, phase, notch filter ran

"""Frequency-domain filtering with the 2-D DFT."""
import numpy as np
from skimage import data, util, metrics, transform


def spectrum(img):
    """Centred log-magnitude spectrum for display."""
    return np.log1p(np.abs(np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft2(img))))


def dist_grid(shape):
    """Distance of every (centred) frequency sample from DC, in cycles per image."""
    H, W = shape
    v = np.fft.fftfreq(H) * H
    u = np.fft.fftfreq(W) * W
    return np.hypot(*np.meshgrid(v, u, indexing="ij"))


def lowpass(shape, d0, kind="gaussian", n=2):
    D = dist_grid(shape)
    if kind == "ideal":
        return (D <= d0).astype(float)
    if kind == "butterworth":
        return 1 / (1 + (D / d0) ** (2 * n))
    return np.exp(-(D ** 2) / (2 * d0 ** 2))


def apply(img, Hf):
    """Multiply the spectrum by a transfer function and invert (filters are zero-phase)."""
    return np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(img) * Hf))


def ringing(img_filtered, img_ref):
    """Overshoot beyond the input's range, as % of that range (ringing proxy)."""
    lo, hi = img_ref.min(), img_ref.max()
    return 100 * max(img_filtered.max() - hi, lo - img_filtered.min(), 0) / (hi - lo)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    f = util.img_as_float(data.camera())
    F = np.fft.fft2(f)
    print(f"DC term / N = {F[0, 0].real / f.size:.4f}   image mean = {f.mean():.4f}")
    print("Parseval holds:", np.isclose((np.abs(F) ** 2).sum() / f.size, (f ** 2).sum()))

    # convolution theorem: circular convolution == pointwise product of spectra
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    k = np.zeros_like(f); k[:5, :5] = rng.random((5, 5))
    direct = np.zeros_like(f)
    for i in range(5):
        for j in range(5):
            direct += k[i, j] * np.roll(f, (i, j), axis=(0, 1))
    print(f"circular conv vs FFT product: max err {np.abs(direct - apply(f, np.fft.fft2(k))).max():.1e}")

    # energy compaction: how much of the (mean-removed) energy lies at low frequencies?
    D, P = dist_grid(f.shape), np.abs(np.fft.fft2(f - f.mean())) ** 2
    for r in (5, 20, 50):
        print(f"energy within radius {r:2d}: {P[D <= r].sum() / P.sum():.4f}")

    # low-pass comparison at the same cut-off
    step = np.zeros((256, 256)); step[:, 128:] = 1
    print(f"{'kind':12s} {'PSNR(cam)':>9s} {'overshoot on step %':>20s}")
    for kind in ("ideal", "butterworth", "gaussian"):
        g = apply(f, lowpass(f.shape, 30, kind))
        s = apply(step, lowpass(step.shape, 15, kind))
        print(f"{kind:12s} {metrics.peak_signal_noise_ratio(f, np.clip(g, 0, 1), data_range=1):9.2f} {ringing(s, step):20.1f}")

    # high-pass = 1 - low-pass; high-boost = 1 + a * high-pass
    hp = apply(f, 1 - lowpass(f.shape, 30))
    print(f"high-pass output mean {hp.mean():.1e} (DC removed), std {hp.std():.3f}")

    # phase carries structure (Oppenheim & Lim)
    g = transform.resize(util.img_as_float(data.astronaut()[..., 1]), f.shape, anti_aliasing=True)
    G = np.fft.fft2(g)
    swap = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.abs(G) * np.exp(1j * np.angle(F))))   # |astronaut|, phase(camera)
    corr = lambda a, b: np.corrcoef(a.ravel(), b.ravel())[0, 1]
    print(f"swap image correlates with camera {corr(swap, f):.2f}, with astronaut {corr(swap, g):.2f}")

    # periodic noise and a notch filter
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:512, :512]
    noisy = f + 0.2 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (24 * xx + 40 * yy) / 512)
    N = np.fft.fft2(noisy)
    mag = np.abs(N); mag[D < 10] = 0                       # ignore the low-frequency bulk
    peaks = np.argwhere(mag > 0.5 * mag.max())
    fr = np.fft.fftfreq(512, 1 / 512)                      # integer frequencies 0..255, -256..-1
    print("detected spike positions (v, u):", [(int(fr[a]), int(fr[b])) for a, b in peaks])
    notch = np.ones(f.shape)
    for a, b in peaks:
        d2 = (fr[:, None] - fr[a]) ** 2 + (fr[None, :] - fr[b]) ** 2
        notch *= 1 - np.exp(-d2 / (2 * 3.0 ** 2))          # Gaussian notch, radius ~3
    clean = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(N * notch))
    psnr = lambda x: metrics.peak_signal_noise_ratio(f, np.clip(x, 0, 1), data_range=1)
    print(f"PSNR noisy {psnr(noisy):.2f} dB -> notch {psnr(clean):.2f} dB  (Gaussian blur s=2 for comparison: "
          f"{psnr(apply(noisy, lowpass(f.shape, 512 / (2 * np.pi * 2)))):.2f} dB)")
DC term / N = 0.5061 image mean = 0.5061 Parseval holds: True circular conv vs FFT product: max err 1.1e-14 energy within radius 5: 0.8056 energy within radius 20: 0.9169 energy within radius 50: 0.9604 kind PSNR(cam) overshoot on step % ideal 22.83 8.9 butterworth 23.62 3.3 gaussian 24.22 0.0 high-pass output mean 2.2e-19 (DC removed), std 0.062 swap image correlates with camera 0.72, with astronaut 0.12 detected spike positions (v, u): [(40, 24), (-40, -24)] PSNR noisy 17.45 dB -> notch 51.52 dB (Gaussian blur s=2 for comparison: 20.97 dB)

4.1 Reading a spectrum

The first lines verify three identities: F[0, 0]/MN is the image mean; Parseval's theorem (energy is the same in both domains); and the convolution theorem, to 10⁻¹⁴. Natural images concentrate their energy at low frequencies: after removing the mean, 81% of the energy of camera lies within 5 cycles per image of DC and 96% within 50, of a possible 256. That compaction is what makes low-pass filtering and transform coding work. Magnitude spectra span many orders of magnitude, so they are displayed as log(1 + |F|) with DC shifted to the centre (Figure 9). The bright horizontal and vertical lines through the centre come largely from the image borders: the DFT treats the image as periodic, and the jump from the right edge back to the left edge is a strong vertical "edge".

Magnitude is not where the structure lives. Oppenheim and Lim showed that an image synthesised from the magnitude of one signal and the phase of another resembles the one that supplied the phase [29]. The experiment reproduces it: |astronaut| combined with the phase of camera correlates 0.72 with the camera image and 0.12 with the astronaut. Phase encodes where edges are; magnitude spectra of natural images are all broadly similar (roughly a 1/f fall-off).

4.2 Low-pass and high-pass filters

Three classical low-pass transfer functions, with D the distance from DC and D₀ the cut-off [1]:

ideal: H = 1 if D ≤ D0, else 0 Butterworth: H = 1 / (1 + (D/D0)^(2n)) Gaussian: H = exp(−D² / 2D0²) high-pass: H_hp = 1 − H_lp

The ideal filter's sharp cut-off sounds optimal but is the worst in practice. Its impulse response is a 2-D sinc-like function (a jinc) with slowly decaying oscillating lobes, so every edge acquires ripples: the output measures an 8.9% overshoot on a step, the Gibbs phenomenon, and the camera image shows rings around the figure (Figure 10). The Butterworth filter (order 2) trades a softer cut-off for a 3.3% overshoot, and the Gaussian has none because its impulse response is a positive Gaussian. A spatial Gaussian of standard deviation σs pixels corresponds to a frequency-domain Gaussian with D₀ = N/(2πσs) cycles per image, which the notch experiment uses for its comparison blur.

4.3 Periodic noise and notch filters

Some degradations are easy in frequency and hard in space. Interference from electrical mains, scanner mechanics or halftone screens adds a sinusoid, which spreads over every pixel but occupies just two points (±(u, v)) in the spectrum. The program adds a sinusoid with 24 cycles horizontally and 40 vertically, finds the two spikes automatically by searching the spectrum outside the low-frequency core, and multiplies by Gaussian notches centred on them. PSNR rises from 17.5 dB to 51.5 dB, essentially perfect, whereas a Gaussian blur strong enough to attenuate the pattern reaches only 21.0 dB because it also destroys image detail (Figure 11).

Practical notes (1) The DFT assumes periodic images, so FFT filtering is circular convolution. To get linear convolution of an M-pixel image with a K-tap kernel, zero-pad (or reflect-pad) both to at least M + K − 1 first. (2) FFTs are fastest for sizes with small prime factors; cv2.getOptimalDFTSize and scipy.fft.next_fast_len return a good padded size. (3) Use rfft2 for real images to halve work and memory. (4) Sampling theory sets the limit on everything in §8 and §9: a band-limited signal can be reconstructed from samples only if it contains no frequencies at or above half the sampling rate [30].
Exercises · §4
  1. For the 512 × 512 camera image, the output reports F[0, 0]/N = 0.5061. What is F[0, 0] itself, and what happens to it under a high-pass filter 1 − H with H(0) = 1?
    Show solution

    F[0, 0] = Σf = 0.5061 × 262,144 ≈ 132,670. Because H(0) = 1, the high-pass gain at DC is 0, so the output mean is 0 (the program prints 2 × 10⁻¹⁹). High-pass images have negative values and must be offset or rescaled for display, or added back to the original (high-boost).

  2. You want to blur a 512 × 512 image with a 31 × 31 kernel via the FFT and obtain the same result as linear convolution with zero padding. What is the minimum padded size, and what size does cv2.getOptimalDFTSize suggest?
    Show solution

    512 + 31 − 1 = 542 per axis. 542 = 2 × 271 has a large prime factor, so the FFT would be relatively slow. cv2.getOptimalDFTSize(542) returns 576 = 2⁶ × 3², the next size whose only prime factors are 2, 3 and 5. Padding to 576 and cropping the result is faster than transforming at 542.

  3. Explain the 8.9% overshoot of the ideal low-pass filter on a step. Would a larger cut-off D₀ reduce it?
    Show solution

    Multiplying by a rectangular H convolves with its inverse transform, a sinc-like kernel with negative lobes; integrating it across a step gives the sine integral, whose maximum exceeds the step by about 9% of the jump. This is the Gibbs phenomenon: increasing D₀ narrows the ripples and moves them closer to the edge, but the peak overshoot stays near 9%. Only a smoother cut-off (Butterworth, Gaussian) reduces it.

  4. Show that a spatial Gaussian with σs = 2 pixels on a 512-pixel axis corresponds to a frequency Gaussian with D₀ ≈ 40.7 cycles per image. Roughly how much is the noise sinusoid at radius √(24² + 40²) attenuated by it?
    Show solution

    The continuous transform of exp(−x²/2σ²) is proportional to exp(−2π²σ²ξ²) with ξ in cycles per pixel. Writing ξ = D/N gives exp(−D²/2D₀²) with D₀ = N/(2πσ) = 512/(4π) ≈ 40.7. The noise lies at D = √(576 + 1600) ≈ 46.6, where H = exp(−46.6²/(2 × 40.7²)) ≈ exp(−0.656) ≈ 0.52: the blur only halves the interference while removing most of the detail above 40 cycles. The notch removes it completely and leaves everything else.

  5. Why does the image built from |G| and the phase of F look like f? Predict what you would see if you kept the phase of F and set every magnitude to 1 ("phase-only" reconstruction).
    Show solution

    Edges and lines are places where many sinusoids align their peaks; the phase determines those alignments, so the phase carries the positions of edges. Natural images have similar, smoothly decaying magnitude spectra, so swapping magnitudes mainly changes the overall contrast balance. Unit magnitudes whiten the spectrum, equalising all frequencies: the reconstruction looks like an edge map of f, with outlines in the right places and flat regions near grey. This whitening is the idea behind phase correlation for image registration.

§5Morphological operations

Mathematical morphology processes images by probing them with a small set called the structuring element (SE) B, and asks set-theoretic questions: does B, placed here, fit inside the object? Does it touch it? Developed by Matheron and Serra for the analysis of mineral sections, it is the natural toolkit for binary masks: cleaning noise, separating or joining objects, filling holes and measuring shapes [31–33].

5.1 Erosion and dilation

For a binary image A (the set of foreground pixels) and a SE B with origin at its centre, with Bx denoting B translated to x:

erosion: A ⊖ B = { x : B_x ⊆ A } (B fits entirely inside A) dilation: A ⊕ B = { x : (B̂)_x ∩ A ≠ ∅ } (reflected B touches A) opening: A ∘ B = (A ⊖ B) ⊕ B (union of all copies of B that fit in A) closing: A • B = (A ⊕ B) ⊖ B (complement of the opening of the background)

Erosion shrinks objects and deletes any part thinner than B; dilation grows them and fills gaps narrower than B. They are dual: eroding the foreground equals dilating the background, (A ⊖ B)c = Ac ⊕ B̂. Opening removes small objects and thin protrusions while restoring the size of everything that survives; closing fills small holes and narrow gaps. Both are idempotent (applying them twice changes nothing), and opening is anti-extensive (A ∘ B ⊆ A) while closing is extensive (A ⊆ A • B) [32]. Figure 12 shows all four on a small shape.

morphology.pyerosion and dilation from the definitions, algebraic checks, coin clean-up, black-hat ran

"""Binary and grey-scale morphology: erosion, dilation, opening, closing and friends."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from scipy import ndimage
from skimage import data, filters, morphology, measure


def erode(A, B):
    """Binary erosion from the definition: keep x where B translated to x fits inside A.
    Outside the image counts as foreground (OpenCV's convention), so borders do not erode."""
    r = np.array(B.shape) // 2
    P = np.pad(A, ((r[0], r[0]), (r[1], r[1])), constant_values=True)
    out = np.ones_like(A, bool)
    for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(B)):
        out &= P[i:i + A.shape[0], j:j + A.shape[1]]
    return out


def dilate(A, B):
    """Binary dilation: the union of copies of A shifted by every point of the reflected B."""
    r = np.array(B.shape) // 2
    P = np.pad(A, ((r[0], r[0]), (r[1], r[1])), constant_values=False)
    out = np.zeros_like(A, bool)
    Bf = B[::-1, ::-1]                    # reflection matters only for asymmetric B
    for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(Bf)):
        out |= P[i:i + A.shape[0], j:j + A.shape[1]]
    return out


opening = lambda A, B: dilate(erode(A, B), B)
closing = lambda A, B: erode(dilate(A, B), B)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
    coins = data.coins()
    A = coins > filters.threshold_otsu(coins)
    A ^= rng.random(A.shape) < 0.02                       # flip 2% of pixels: salt and pepper
    B = morphology.disk(2)

    print("ours == scipy erosion :", np.array_equal(erode(A, B), ndimage.binary_erosion(A, B, border_value=1)))
    print("ours == scipy dilation:", np.array_equal(dilate(A, B), ndimage.binary_dilation(A, B)))
    print("duality (A erode B)^c == A^c dilate B:", np.array_equal(~erode(A, B), dilate(~A, B)))
    O = opening(A, B)
    print("opening idempotent:", np.array_equal(opening(O, B), O),
          " anti-extensive:", not (O & ~A).any(), " closing extensive:", not (A & ~closing(A, B)).any())

    for name, X in [("thresholded + noise", A), ("open", O), ("open then close", closing(O, B)),
                    ("open, close, fill holes", ndimage.binary_fill_holes(closing(O, B)))]:
        lab = measure.label(X)
        sizes = np.bincount(lab.ravel())[1:]
        print(f"{name:24s}: {lab.max():4d} components, {np.sum(sizes >= 200):2d} of them >= 200 px, holes px "
              f"{(ndimage.binary_fill_holes(X) & ~X).sum():5d}")

    # grey-scale: gradient and top-hat on uneven illumination
    page = data.page()
    grad = cv2.morphologyEx(page, cv2.MORPH_GRADIENT, np.ones((3, 3), np.uint8))
    bh = cv2.morphologyEx(page, cv2.MORPH_BLACKHAT, cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (15, 15)))
    bg = cv2.morphologyEx(page, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (15, 15)))
    print("black-hat == closing - image:", np.array_equal(bh, bg - page))
    for name, im in [("page", page), ("background (closing)", bg)]:
        print(f"{name:21s} column means left/right: {im[:, :60].mean():.0f} / {im[:, -60:].mean():.0f}")
    print(f"gradient: mean {grad.mean():.1f}, 99th percentile {np.percentile(grad, 99):.0f}")
    ink = bh > filters.threshold_otsu(bh)
    print(f"ink fraction after black-hat + Otsu: {ink.mean():.3f}")

The implementations follow the definitions literally: erosion is the AND of shifted copies of A, one per SE pixel, and dilation is the OR. Both match SciPy, and the duality, idempotence and (anti-)extensivity properties hold exactly. One subtlety is the border: what lies outside the image? OpenCV treats it as foreground for erosion and background for dilation, so that neither operation creates artefacts at the edges; our erosion pads with True for the same reason, and the closing is only extensive under that convention.

5.2 Cleaning a binary mask

The second block simulates a noisy segmentation: Otsu's mask of coins with 2% of the pixels flipped. It has 1,235 connected components although the image contains 24 coins. Opening with a radius-2 disk removes every speck smaller than the disk (1,235 → 31 components); closing then reconnects coins fragmented by pepper noise (25), and hole filling, a morphological reconstruction from the border [34], removes the dark interiors of the coins. The 24 large components are the 24 coins; the remaining one is a small fragment of under-segmented coin edge (Figure 13).

5.3 Grey-scale morphology

For grey-level images, erosion and dilation with a flat SE become the local minimum and maximum over the SE. Opening then removes bright structures smaller than the SE, closing removes dark ones, and several useful operators follow [33]:

  • Morphological gradient, dilation − erosion: the local range, a robust edge strength.
  • White top-hat, f − (f ∘ B): bright details smaller than B on a slowly varying background.
  • Black-hat, (f • B) − f: dark details smaller than B, such as text on paper.

On page, a closing with a 15 × 15 disk erases the text strokes (narrower than the disk) and leaves an estimate of the paper's shading (Figure 14). Subtracting the image from it, the black-hat, gives a text image whose background is near zero everywhere, and a plain global Otsu threshold on it labels 10.3% of pixels as ink without being fooled by the dark left margin. The capstone in §10 uses the same background estimate, with division instead of subtraction. A min or max over a k-pixel line costs O(1) per pixel regardless of k with the van Herk/Gil–Werman algorithm, so even large rectangular structuring elements are cheap [35].

Exercises · §5
  1. Erode and dilate the 1-D signal 0011111000110 with the 3-pixel SE 111 (outside counts as foreground for erosion, background for dilation). Then compute the opening and closing.
    Show solution

    Erosion keeps a pixel only if it and both neighbours are 1: 0001110000000 (the 2-pixel run disappears). Dilation sets a pixel if any of the three is 1: 0111111101111. Opening = dilate(erosion) = 0011111000000: the 5-run is restored exactly and the 2-run, too short to hold the SE, is gone. Closing = erode(dilation) = 0011111000111: the gap of three zeros between the runs survives (it is as wide as the SE), but the 2-run grows by one pixel to the right edge, because outside the signal counts as foreground for the erosion. These values were checked with SciPy.

  2. Prove that opening is idempotent: (A ∘ B) ∘ B = A ∘ B.
    Show solution

    Use the characterisation A ∘ B = ∪{Bx : Bx ⊆ A}. Let O = A ∘ B. Opening is anti-extensive, so O ∘ B ⊆ O. Conversely, every translate Bx ⊆ A that makes up O is also contained in O (since O is their union), so it appears in the union defining O ∘ B; hence O ⊆ O ∘ B. Both inclusions give equality. Idempotence is what makes opening a filter in the morphological sense: once applied, it has done all it can.

  3. Dilating by a 3 × 3 square seven times equals one dilation by what SE? Compare the cost per pixel with a direct dilation by that SE, and with two 1-D line passes.
    Show solution

    Dilation is associative: (A ⊕ B₁) ⊕ B₂ = A ⊕ (B₁ ⊕ B₂), and seven 3 × 3 squares combine into a 15 × 15 square. Direct: 225 comparisons per pixel; seven passes: 7 × 9 = 63; the square is also separable into a 15 × 1 and a 1 × 15 line (30 comparisons), and with van Herk's algorithm each line costs about 3 comparisons per pixel independent of length [35].

  4. You need to remove noise specks up to 3 pixels across from a mask of cells that are at least 20 pixels across, and also to fill pinholes up to 2 pixels wide inside the cells. Which operations and SE sizes do you choose, and in which order?
    Show solution

    Opening with a disk of diameter 5 (radius 2) removes anything that cannot contain the disk, so 3-pixel specks vanish while 20-pixel cells are restored. A closing with a disk of radius 1–2 then fills pinholes up to about 2–3 pixels wide. Open first so the closing does not merge noise specks into the cells. If holes can be larger but are fully enclosed, hole filling by reconstruction is better than a large closing, which would also merge touching cells.

  5. For dark text on a light, unevenly lit page, would you use the white top-hat or the black-hat, and how large should the SE be?
    Show solution

    The black-hat, (f • B) − f, because the features of interest are dark. The closing must remove the strokes completely, so the SE must be wider than the thickest stroke (a little over the stroke width; 15 × 15 is generous for page), yet small compared with the scale of the illumination change so that the background estimate follows the shading. The white top-hat would extract bright features such as paper texture and glare.

§6Image enhancement

Enhancement makes an image more useful for a particular viewer or algorithm, with no ground truth to aim at: success is judged by the result [1]. Its two main tasks are adjusting contrast, which uses the point operations of §1 chosen automatically from the image's statistics, and removing noise, which uses and extends the filters of §3.

6.1 Contrast adjustment and histogram equalisation

The linear and gamma adjustments of §1 need parameters. Histogram equalisation chooses the transfer function from the data: map each level through the image's own cumulative distribution function (CDF). For a continuous variable r with CDF c(r), the variable s = c(r) is uniformly distributed, so the output uses all levels equally often. For 8-bit images:

s_k = round( (cdf(k) − cdf_min) / (N − cdf_min) · 255 ) cdf(k) = number of pixels with level ≤ k

Levels that hold many pixels are spread apart and sparse levels are squeezed together, which raises contrast where most pixels lie. Our implementation matches cv2.equalizeHist exactly. Equalisation is global and blunt: on moon the standard deviation jumps from 13.3 to 74.0, but the output uses only 49 distinct levels (178 were used before), the discrete histogram is far from flat (24% of pixels lie below level 64 rather than 25%, but 45% below 128 and 74% below 192), and the entropy falls slightly, as exercise 5 of §1 predicts. Noise in large flat regions is amplified along with everything else.

Adaptive histogram equalisation (AHE) computes a separate mapping from the histogram of each pixel's neighbourhood, so local contrast is enhanced everywhere [36]. Unconstrained, it turns the noise of flat regions into strong texture, because a near-constant region has a narrow histogram that equalisation stretches to the full range. Contrast-limited AHE (CLAHE) clips each local histogram at a limit and redistributes the excess equally over all bins before computing the CDF, which caps the slope of the mapping and thus the noise gain; mappings are computed per tile and bilinearly interpolated between tile centres to avoid block artefacts [36,37]. CLAHE is not a point operation (the same input level maps differently in different tiles), which is why its output uses 246 levels and its entropy rises to 5.83 bits.

enhance.pyhistogram equalisation, CLAHE, six denoisers scored with PSNR and SSIM ran

"""Contrast enhancement and denoising, scored against a clean reference."""
import time
import numpy as np
import cv2
from skimage import data, exposure, restoration, util, metrics


def equalize(img):
    """Global histogram equalisation for uint8: map each level through the normalised CDF."""
    hist = np.bincount(img.ravel(), minlength=256)
    cdf = hist.cumsum()
    cdf_min = cdf[cdf > 0][0]
    lut = np.round((cdf - cdf_min) / (cdf[-1] - cdf_min) * 255).clip(0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
    return lut[img]


def entropy_bits(img):
    p = np.bincount(img.ravel(), minlength=256) / img.size
    p = p[p > 0]
    return -(p * np.log2(p)).sum()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    moon = data.moon()
    eq = equalize(moon)
    print("ours == cv2.equalizeHist:", np.array_equal(eq, cv2.equalizeHist(moon)))
    clahe = cv2.createCLAHE(clipLimit=2.0, tileGridSize=(8, 8)).apply(moon)
    for name, im in [("original", moon), ("equalised", eq), ("CLAHE clip=2 8x8", clahe)]:
        print(f"{name:17s} std={im.std():5.1f}  levels used={len(np.unique(im)):3d}  entropy={entropy_bits(im):.2f} bits")
    h = np.bincount(eq.ravel(), minlength=256)
    print("equalised CDF at 64/128/192:", np.round(h.cumsum()[[63, 127, 191]] / eq.size, 3))

    # denoising
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    clean = util.img_as_float(data.astronaut()[100:356, 140:396])        # 256x256 colour crop
    sigma = 0.08
    noisy = np.clip(clean + rng.normal(0, sigma, clean.shape), 0, 1)
    est = restoration.estimate_sigma(noisy, channel_axis=-1, average_sigmas=True)
    print(f"true sigma {sigma}, wavelet-MAD estimate {est:.3f}")
    u8 = lambda x: (x * 255).round().astype(np.uint8)
    methods = {
        "noisy input":     lambda x: x,
        "Gaussian s=1":    lambda x: cv2.GaussianBlur(x, (0, 0), 1.0),
        "bilateral":       lambda x: cv2.bilateralFilter(x.astype(np.float32), 7, 0.2, 2),
        "TV (Chambolle)":  lambda x: restoration.denoise_tv_chambolle(x, weight=0.08, channel_axis=-1),
        "wavelet (BayesShrink)": lambda x: restoration.denoise_wavelet(x, channel_axis=-1, convert2ycbcr=True,
                                                                     method="BayesShrink", mode="soft", rescale_sigma=True),
        "NL-means (skimage)": lambda x: restoration.denoise_nl_means(x, h=0.8 * est, sigma=est, fast_mode=True,
                                                                     patch_size=5, patch_distance=6, channel_axis=-1),
        "NL-means (OpenCV)": lambda x: cv2.fastNlMeansDenoisingColored(u8(x), None, 16, 16, 7, 21) / 255.0,
    }
    print(f"{'method':22s} {'PSNR':>6s} {'SSIM':>6s} {'ms':>6s}")
    for name, fn in methods.items():
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); y = np.clip(fn(noisy), 0, 1); dt = 1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0)
        p = metrics.peak_signal_noise_ratio(clean, y, data_range=1)
        s = metrics.structural_similarity(clean, y, data_range=1, channel_axis=-1)
        print(f"{name:22s} {p:6.2f} {s:6.3f} {dt:6.0f}")

6.2 Denoising

Sensor noise is the dominant degradation in low light. For evaluation it is usually modelled as additive white Gaussian noise of known σ, although real camera noise is signal-dependent (shot noise is Poisson) and spatially correlated after demosaicing. Modern classical denoisers exploit a stronger prior than "images are smooth":

  • Total variation (TV) denoising minimises ½‖u − f‖² + λ·TV(u), where TV(u) = Σ|∇u|. The L1 penalty on gradients prefers piecewise-constant images: flat regions are smoothed hard, but large jumps cost only their height, so edges survive [38]. The typical artefact is "staircasing" of smooth gradients into flat terraces.
  • Wavelet shrinkage transforms to a wavelet basis, where natural images are sparse and white noise is not, shrinks small coefficients towards zero and transforms back [39]. The noise level itself can be estimated robustly from the finest-scale diagonal coefficients as median(|d|)/0.6745; the program's estimate is 0.074 for a true σ of 0.08.
  • Non-local means (NL-means) averages pixels whose surrounding patches look alike, wherever they are in a search window, rather than pixels that are merely close [40]. Natural images are full of repeated structure (texture, edges along their length), so many good matches exist.
  • BM3D groups similar patches into 3-D stacks, filters each stack jointly in a transform domain and aggregates the results; it was the classical state of the art for Gaussian noise for a decade [41]. Learned denoisers such as DnCNN, trained on pairs of clean and noisy images, now exceed it [42].

On a 256 × 256 colour crop with σ = 0.08, NL-means gives the best PSNR (30.3 dB) and SSIM (0.838), and TV is second on both (Figure 16). The two metrics do not always agree: the bilateral filter and the wavelet denoiser beat the Gaussian blur on PSNR (28.3 and 28.2 dB against 27.2 dB) but lose to it on SSIM (0.711 and 0.730 against 0.756), because SSIM penalises the blotchy residual structure they leave in flat regions more than the uniform softness of a blur [7]. OpenCV's fastNlMeansDenoisingColored, run here with untuned strength h = 16 on 8-bit data, scored lower than scikit-image's NL-means; NL-means results depend strongly on h relative to σ, and the comparison is about parameters, not libraries. Timings are wall-clock on one CPU core and indicate relative cost only.

Exercises · §6
  1. A 3-bit image (levels 0–7) of 100 pixels has histogram counts (0, 0, 40, 30, 20, 10, 0, 0). Equalise it with the formula above (using 7 instead of 255).
    Show solution

    CDF: (0, 0, 40, 70, 90, 100, 100, 100), cdfmin = 40. s = round((cdf − 40)/60 × 7): level 2 → 0, level 3 → round(3.5) = 4, level 4 → round(5.83) = 6, level 5 → 7. The four occupied levels now span the full range 0–7, with the gaps largest where the counts were largest (between 2 and 3), but four levels remain four levels: the histogram is spread, not flattened.

  2. Why does global equalisation of moon reduce the number of distinct levels from 178 to 49?
    Show solution

    Most of moon's pixels sit in a narrow band of levels, and many levels hold only a few pixels. Consecutive sparse levels have nearly equal CDF values, so after scaling to 0–255 and rounding they map to the same output level. Equalisation is a monotonic many-to-one map on a discrete set; it can merge bins but never split them, so the number of levels can only stay the same or fall.

  3. In CLAHE, what happens in the limits clip limit → ∞ and clip limit → its minimum (each bin capped at the uniform level)?
    Show solution

    With no clipping, CLAHE becomes plain tile-wise AHE with bilinear blending, with maximal local contrast and maximal noise amplification in flat tiles. When every bin is clipped to the uniform height, the redistributed histogram is flat, its CDF is a straight line, and the mapping is the identity: no enhancement. The clip limit interpolates between these extremes by bounding the maximum slope of each tile's mapping.

  4. Convert the PSNRs of the noisy input (22.47 dB) and of NL-means (30.33 dB) into RMS errors on the [0, 1] scale. By what factor did NL-means reduce the RMS error?
    Show solution

    RMSE = 10−PSNR/20: 10−1.1235 = 0.0752 for the input (slightly below σ = 0.08 because clipping to [0, 1] removed some noise) and 10−1.5165 = 0.0304 after NL-means. The error fell by a factor of 2.47, about 7.9 dB.

  5. The TV-denoised image shows flat patches on the cheek where the clean image has a smooth shading gradient. Explain this with the TV penalty, and name a regulariser that avoids it.
    Show solution

    TV penalises Σ|∇u|, the total height climbed. A ramp from 0 to h and a single step from 0 to h have the same total variation, so TV is indifferent between them; combined with the data term and noise, the minimiser tends to choose piecewise-constant solutions, which shows up as staircasing on gentle gradients. Total generalised variation (TGV), which also penalises second derivatives, or a Huber-smoothed TV, favours piecewise-smooth rather than piecewise-constant images and reduces the effect.

§7Image restoration

Restoration differs from enhancement in having an objective target: the image that would have been recorded without the degradation. It starts from a model of how the image was degraded and tries to invert it [1,14,43]. The standard linear model (Figure 17) is a convolution with a point-spread function (PSF) h plus noise:

g = h ∗ f + n ⇔ G(u, v) = H(u, v) · F(u, v) + N(u, v)

7.1 Deblurring: inverse, Wiener and Richardson–Lucy

The naive inverse filter divides the spectrum by H: F̂ = G/H = F + N/H. Without noise it is exact. With noise, every frequency where |H| is tiny multiplies the noise by a huge factor. A motion-blur PSF is a line segment whose transform is a sinc along the motion direction with exact zeros; the program's 15-pixel blur has |H| as small as 10⁻⁶, and 5% of frequencies have |H| < 0.01.

The Wiener filter is the linear filter that minimises the expected squared error E|f − f̂|² when signal and noise are stationary random processes [44]:

F̂ = [ H* / (|H|² + S_n/S_f) ] · G (constant K replaces S_n/S_f when the spectra are unknown)

Where the signal-to-noise ratio is high it acts as the inverse filter; where |H|² falls below the noise-to-signal ratio it rolls off towards zero instead of exploding. Richardson–Lucy (R–L) deconvolution, derived independently for optics and astronomy, is the maximum-likelihood estimate under Poisson (photon-counting) noise, computed by multiplicative updates that keep the image non-negative [45,46]:

f̂ ← f̂ · [ h̃ ∗ ( g / (h ∗ f̂) ) ] h̃ = h flipped (correlation with the PSF)

restore.pymotion blur, inverse/Wiener/Richardson–Lucy deconvolution, three inpainting methods ran

"""Restoration: undo a known blur (deconvolution) and fill missing pixels (inpainting)."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from skimage import data, util, metrics, restoration


def motion_psf(length=15, angle=30, size=31):
    """Linear motion-blur point-spread function, normalised to sum 1."""
    k = np.zeros((size, size)); c = size // 2
    t = np.deg2rad(angle)
    for s in np.linspace(-(length - 1) / 2, (length - 1) / 2, 4 * length):
        k[int(round(c - s * np.sin(t))), int(round(c + s * np.cos(t)))] = 1
    return k / k.sum()


def psf2otf(psf, shape):
    """Zero-pad the PSF to the image size and circularly shift its centre to (0, 0)."""
    P = np.zeros(shape); P[:psf.shape[0], :psf.shape[1]] = psf
    P = np.roll(P, (-(psf.shape[0] // 2), -(psf.shape[1] // 2)), axis=(0, 1))
    return np.fft.fft2(P)


def inverse_filter(g, psf, eps=0.0):
    H = psf2otf(psf, g.shape)
    Hs = np.where(np.abs(H) < eps, eps, H) if eps else H
    return np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(g) / Hs))


def wiener(g, psf, nsr):
    """Wiener deconvolution with a constant noise-to-signal power ratio K."""
    H = psf2otf(psf, g.shape)
    W = np.conj(H) / (np.abs(H) ** 2 + nsr)
    return np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(g) * W))


def blur(f, psf):          # circular blur, so that the frequency-domain model is exact
    return np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(f) * psf2otf(psf, f.shape)))


def richardson_lucy(g, psf, n_iter=30):
    """Multiplicative ML updates for Poisson noise: x <- x * H^T (g / H x)."""
    H = psf2otf(psf, g.shape)
    x = np.full(g.shape, g.mean())
    for _ in range(n_iter):
        ratio = g / np.maximum(np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(x) * H)), 1e-6)
        x *= np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.fft.fft2(ratio) * np.conj(H)))   # correlate with the PSF
    return x


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

    for sigma in (0.0, 0.01):

        print(f"  inverse, |H|>=0.05   {PS(inverse_filter(g, psf, 0.05)):6.2f} dB")

        for n in (10, 30, 100):
            print(f"  Richardson-Lucy x{n:<3d} {PS(richardson_lucy(np.clip(g, 0, None), psf, n)):6.2f} dB")
    sk = restoration.wiener(g, psf, balance=1e-2, clip=False)   # skimage's Wiener-Hunt (Laplacian regulariser)
    print(f"  skimage Wiener-Hunt  {PS(sk):6.2f} dB  (Laplacian smoothness prior instead of constant K)")

    # inpainting: remove scribbled strokes and fill them in

        p1, p2 = rng.integers(0, 512, 2), rng.integers(0, 512, 2)
        cv2.line(mask, tuple(map(int, p1)), tuple(map(int, p2)), 255, int(rng.integers(3, 9)))

    def score(x):
        x = util.img_as_float(x)
        return metrics.peak_signal_noise_ratio(ref[m], x[m], data_range=1)
    out = {
        "damaged (white)":  damaged,
        "Telea (cv2)":      cv2.inpaint(damaged, mask, 5, cv2.INPAINT_TELEA),
        "Navier-Stokes":    cv2.inpaint(damaged, mask, 5, cv2.INPAINT_NS),
        "biharmonic (skimage)": restoration.inpaint_biharmonic(damaged, m, channel_axis=-1),
