The results lay out the trade-off. With no noise, the inverse filter recovers the image to floating-point precision (257 dB) and Wiener with the smallest K is best of the rest. Adding noise of σ = 0.01, barely visible, sends the inverse filter to 4.8 dB, worse than doing nothing. Wiener needs a larger K (0.01 is best of the three tried, 25.6 dB), and scikit-image's Wiener–Hunt variant, which uses a Laplacian smoothness prior instead of a constant K, reaches 27.5 dB. R–L shows semi-convergence: with noise its PSNR rises to 26.5 dB at 30 iterations and falls to 24.9 dB at 100 as it starts fitting the noise, so the iteration count acts as the regularisation parameter (Figure 18). The model here is exactly circular so that the frequency-domain filters are not penalised at the borders; with real data, boundary handling (edge tapering or padding) matters.

When the PSF is unknown, the problem is blind deconvolution: estimate h and f together. It is badly under-determined (the pair (f, δ) explains any image), so methods rely on strong priors, such as the heavy-tailed gradient statistics of natural images used by Fergus et al. to remove camera shake [47]. Levin et al. showed why naive MAP estimation of both unknowns favours the blurry "no-blur" solution, and that estimating the kernel first, marginalising over images, works better [48].

7.2 Inpainting

Inpainting fills a region Ω of missing or unwanted pixels (scratches, text overlays, removed objects) from the surrounding image. Bertalmio et al. introduced the term in image processing and a PDE that propagates image information along isophotes (lines of constant intensity) into the hole [49], and later related it to the Navier–Stokes equations of fluid flow, with image intensity playing the role of a stream function [50]. Telea's method fills the hole from its boundary inwards in fast-marching order, each new pixel being a weighted average of known neighbours [51]; both are in OpenCV as INPAINT_TELEA and INPAINT_NS. Biharmonic inpainting solves ∇⁴u = 0 in Ω, giving the smoothest surface that matches the boundary values and their slopes [52].

All three are diffusion-type methods: they continue smooth structure and edges into thin regions well, but cannot invent texture, and they blur over large holes. On 25 random strokes covering 16% of astronaut, they reach 19.8–20.9 dB on the masked pixels (Figure 19), with biharmonic best. Large holes need methods that copy or synthesise texture: exemplar-based inpainting copies whole patches from elsewhere in the image, filling in an order that prioritises continuing linear structures [53], and learned inpainting networks such as LaMa, which uses Fourier convolutions for an image-wide receptive field, handle large masks [54].

7.3 Choosing a noise remover by noise model

"Noise removal" spans enhancement and restoration; the right tool is set by the noise model, and every section so far has contributed one:

NoiseSignatureToolMeasured here
Impulse (salt and pepper)isolated extreme pixelsmedian (§3); adaptive median15.8 → 27.8 dB
Additive Gaussian, whitefine grain everywhereNL-means, BM3D, TV, wavelets, CNNs (§6)22.5 → 30.3 dB
Periodic interferenceisolated spectral peaksnotch filter (§4)17.5 → 51.5 dB
Blur + noiseloss of high frequenciesWiener, R–L, regularised deconvolution (§7)23.1 → 27.5 dB
Missing pixelsknown maskinpainting (§7)3.8 → 20.9 dB (masked)
Exercises · §7
  1. Show that the Wiener filter reduces to the inverse filter when K = 0 and to zero where |H|² ≪ K. Why is K = 0.01 better than 10⁻⁴ for noise σ = 0.01?
    Show solution

    With K = 0, H*/|H|² = 1/H. Where |H|² ≪ K, H*/(|H|² + K) ≈ H*/K → 0 as |H| → 0. K stands for the noise-to-signal power ratio. The noise power per frequency is flat (σ² × number of pixels in NumPy's unnormalised DFT), while image power falls steeply with frequency, so at mid and high frequencies the true ratio is much larger than 10⁻⁴; with 10⁻⁴ the filter still divides by |H| at frequencies that are mostly noise. A frequency-dependent K(u, v) from a model of the image spectrum is better than any constant, which is what the Laplacian prior of Wiener–Hunt approximates.

  2. A horizontal motion blur of L pixels has a 1-D transfer function proportional to sin(πuL/N)/sin(πu/N). For N = 512 and L = 16, at which frequencies is H zero? What does this mean for any deconvolution?
    Show solution

    Zeros where uL/N is a non-zero integer and u/N is not: u = 32, 64, 96, … cycles per image. At those frequencies the blurred image contains only noise, so no linear filter can recover F there; the information is gone. Deconvolution can at best restore the other frequencies and fill the zeros from a prior (smoothness, sparsity, learned image statistics). Coded-exposure cameras flutter the shutter to make the motion PSF broadband, with no zeros, for exactly this reason.

  3. Richardson–Lucy's PSNR with noise rose from 25.6 dB (10 iterations) to 26.5 dB (30), then fell to 24.9 dB (100). Explain, and propose a rule for choosing the iteration count without the ground truth.
    Show solution

    Early iterations restore the low and middle frequencies, where the signal dominates; later iterations push towards the maximum-likelihood fit of the noisy data, which means reconstructing high frequencies where H is small and the data are mostly noise. The error therefore first falls and then rises (semi-convergence). Without ground truth, stop when the residual g − h ∗ f̂ becomes statistically consistent with the known noise level (the discrepancy principle: ‖residual‖² ≈ number of pixels × σ²), or add an explicit regulariser such as TV to the R–L update.

  4. Why does the inverse filter give 257 dB without noise rather than "infinite" dB, given |H| as small as 10⁻⁶?
    Show solution

    With σ = 0, the blurred image g is computed in double precision, so G = H F up to rounding errors of order 10⁻¹⁶ relative. Dividing by |H| ≈ 10⁻⁶ amplifies those rounding errors by 10⁶, leaving errors around 10⁻¹³ in the image: PSNR = 20 log10(1/RMSE) ≈ 257 dB corresponds to RMSE ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻¹³. Any real noise, even quantisation to 8 bits (σ ≈ 0.0011), is ten orders of magnitude larger.

  5. You must remove a 120 × 80-pixel logo from the middle of a photograph of grass. Which of Telea, biharmonic, exemplar-based and learned inpainting would you choose, and why?
    Show solution

    The hole is large and the surroundings are stochastic texture. Diffusion methods (Telea, Navier–Stokes, biharmonic) would produce a smooth green blur that is obviously wrong. Exemplar-based inpainting copies real grass patches from the rest of the image and would look plausible [53]; a learned large-mask model such as LaMa [54] would also work well and copes better with structure such as a horizon crossing the hole. Diffusion is the right choice for thin scratches and small specks.

§8Geometric operations

Geometric operations move pixels instead of changing their values: rotation, scaling, cropping, flipping, shearing, perspective correction, lens-distortion removal. Each is defined by a coordinate transform T that maps input positions p = (x, y) to output positions q = T(p). Two problems must be solved: computing T, and resampling the image on the new grid, which requires interpolation and, when shrinking, anti-aliasing [2,55].

8.1 Transforms as matrices

In homogeneous coordinates (x, y, 1), all the common planar transforms are 3 × 3 matrices, and composing transforms is matrix multiplication [56]:

TransformMatrix (top two rows; last row 0 0 1 unless stated)DOFPreserves
Translation[1 0 t_x; 0 1 t_y]2everything but position
Euclidean (rotation + translation)[cos θ −sin θ t_x; sin θ cos θ t_y]3lengths, angles
Similarity (+ uniform scale)[s cos θ −s sin θ t_x; s sin θ s cos θ t_y]4angles, length ratios
Affine[a b t_x; c d t_y]6parallelism, area ratios
Projective (homography)[h11 h12 h13; h21 h22 h23; h31 h32 1]8straight lines, cross-ratio

Cropping is a translation (and in NumPy, a slice); flipping is a scale by −1. Rotation "about the centre" is translate–rotate–translate, which rot_about builds explicitly and verifies against cv2.getRotationMatrix2D. Because the image y axis points down, a matrix that is a counter-clockwise rotation in ordinary maths coordinates turns content clockwise on screen; OpenCV defines its angle so that positive values rotate counter-clockwise as displayed, which is why its matrix has the sign pattern used in the code. A homography maps the image of a plane under any pinhole camera motion, so it rectifies photographed documents, screens and façades; it has 8 degrees of freedom and is determined by four point correspondences, no three collinear [56].

8.2 Forward versus inverse mapping

The obvious implementation, forward mapping, pushes each input pixel to round(T(p)). It leaves holes wherever the output grid is not hit, and collisions where it is hit twice: for a 30° rotation, 13.5% of the covered output pixels are never written (Figure 21, top left). Inverse mapping loops over output pixels instead, computes p = T⁻¹(q), and samples the input there. Every output pixel gets exactly one value, at the price of evaluating the image at non-integer positions, so it needs an interpolation rule. All library warps work this way; cv2.warpAffine takes the forward matrix and inverts it internally unless the WARP_INVERSE_MAP flag is given.

8.3 Interpolation

Interpolation reconstructs a continuous image from samples by convolving them with a kernel, then samples it at the new positions [57,58]:

  • Nearest neighbour: copy the closest sample. Fast, introduces no new values (essential for label maps and masks), but jagged.
  • Bilinear: the tent kernel over 2 × 2 neighbours (Figure 20). Continuous but blurs, because the tent kernel attenuates high frequencies.
  • Bicubic: Keys' cubic convolution over 4 × 4 neighbours, with a free parameter a (OpenCV uses −0.75, Keys recommended −0.5) [59]. Sharper, with slight overshoot. Mitchell and Netravali analysed the family of cubic filters as a trade-off between blur, ringing and anisotropy [60].
  • Lanczos: a sinc windowed by a wider sinc, over 8 × 8 neighbours in OpenCV's INTER_LANCZOS4 [61]. Closest to ideal band-limited reconstruction, at the cost of more ringing and computation.

geometry.pyrotation matrices, forward vs inverse warping, interpolation, aliasing, perspective, cropping ran

"""Geometric transforms: matrices, inverse mapping, interpolation and aliasing."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from skimage import data, util, metrics


def rot_about(theta_deg, cx, cy, s=1.0):
    """3x3 homogeneous matrix: translate centre to origin, rotate+scale, translate back.
    Image axes: x right, y down, so a positive angle turns the content counter-clockwise on screen."""
    t = np.deg2rad(theta_deg)
    T1 = np.array([[1, 0, -cx], [0, 1, -cy], [0, 0, 1]])
    R = np.array([[s * np.cos(t), s * np.sin(t), 0], [-s * np.sin(t), s * np.cos(t), 0], [0, 0, 1]])
    T2 = np.array([[1, 0, cx], [0, 1, cy], [0, 0, 1]])
    return T2 @ R @ T1


def warp_forward(img, M):
    """Forward mapping: push every source pixel to round(M @ p). Leaves holes."""
    H, W = img.shape
    out = np.full((H, W), np.nan)
    ys, xs = np.mgrid[:H, :W]
    p = M @ np.stack([xs.ravel(), ys.ravel(), np.ones(H * W)])
    u, v = np.round(p[0] / p[2]).astype(int), np.round(p[1] / p[2]).astype(int)
    ok = (u >= 0) & (u < W) & (v >= 0) & (v < H)
    out[v[ok], u[ok]] = img.ravel()[ok]
    return out


def warp_inverse_bilinear(img, M):
    """Inverse mapping: for every output pixel, sample the source at M^-1 @ q bilinearly."""
    H, W = img.shape
    Minv = np.linalg.inv(M)
    ys, xs = np.mgrid[:H, :W]
    q = Minv @ np.stack([xs.ravel(), ys.ravel(), np.ones(H * W)])
    x, y = q[0] / q[2], q[1] / q[2]
    x0, y0 = np.floor(x).astype(int), np.floor(y).astype(int)
    a, b = x - x0, y - y0
    ok = (x0 >= 0) & (x0 < W - 1) & (y0 >= 0) & (y0 < H - 1)
    x0, y0, a, b = x0[ok], y0[ok], a[ok], b[ok]
    val = ((1 - a) * (1 - b) * img[y0, x0] + a * (1 - b) * img[y0, x0 + 1] +
           (1 - a) * b * img[y0 + 1, x0] + a * b * img[y0 + 1, x0 + 1])
    out = np.zeros(H * W); out[ok] = val
    return out.reshape(H, W)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    f = util.img_as_float(data.camera())
    M = rot_about(30, 255.5, 255.5)
    M_cv = cv2.getRotationMatrix2D((255.5, 255.5), 30, 1.0)
    print("our matrix matches cv2.getRotationMatrix2D:", np.allclose(M[:2], M_cv))

    fw = warp_forward(f, M)
    inside = warp_inverse_bilinear(np.ones_like(f), M) > 0.999
    print(f"forward mapping: {np.isnan(fw[inside]).mean():.1%} of covered output pixels are holes")
    ours = warp_inverse_bilinear(f, M)
    ocv = cv2.warpAffine(f, M_cv, (512, 512), flags=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
    print(f"inverse bilinear vs cv2.warpAffine: max diff {np.abs(ours - ocv)[inside].max():.1e}")

    # accumulated error: rotate 12 times by 30 degrees (= 360), compare with the original
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:512, :512]
    disc = (xx - 255.5) ** 2 + (yy - 255.5) ** 2 < 200 ** 2          # region that never leaves the frame
    flags = {"nearest": cv2.INTER_NEAREST, "bilinear": cv2.INTER_LINEAR,
             "bicubic": cv2.INTER_CUBIC, "Lanczos-4": cv2.INTER_LANCZOS4}
    for name, fl in flags.items():
        x = f.copy()
        for _ in range(12):
            x = cv2.warpAffine(x, M_cv, (512, 512), flags=fl, borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
        print(f"{name:10s} after 12 x 30 deg: PSNR {metrics.peak_signal_noise_ratio(f[disc], np.clip(x, 0, 1)[disc], data_range=1):6.2f} dB")

    # downsampling: aliasing without a low-pass prefilter
    r = np.hypot(xx - 256, yy - 256)
    zone = 0.5 + 0.5 * np.cos(np.pi * r ** 2 / 512)                 # zone plate: frequency grows with radius
    for name, small in [("nearest (decimate)", zone[::4, ::4]),
                        ("INTER_AREA", cv2.resize(zone, (128, 128), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)),
                        ("Gaussian then decimate", cv2.GaussianBlur(zone, (0, 0), 1.6)[::4, ::4])]:
        ring = small[np.hypot(*np.mgrid[:128, :128] - 64) > 40]       # beyond the new Nyquist radius
        print(f"{name:23s} contrast beyond new Nyquist (std): {ring.std():.3f}")

    # perspective: rectify a page photographed at an angle
    page = data.page()
    h, w = page.shape
    src = np.float32([[0, 0], [w, 0], [w, h], [0, h]])
    dst = np.float32([[40, 30], [w - 10, 0], [w - 50, h + 20], [0, h - 25]])
    Hm = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(src, dst)
    shot = cv2.warpPerspective(page, Hm, (w, h + 30), flags=cv2.INTER_CUBIC)
    Hinv = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(dst, src)
    back = cv2.warpPerspective(shot, Hinv, (w, h), flags=cv2.INTER_CUBIC)
    print("H @ H_inv ~ I (scaled):", np.allclose(Hm @ Hinv / (Hm @ Hinv)[2, 2], np.eye(3), atol=1e-9))
    print(f"rectified page: mean abs error {np.abs(back[5:-5, 5:-5].astype(int) - page[5:-5, 5:-5]).mean():.2f} grey levels")

    # cropping is slicing: a view, not a copy
    crop = f[100:200, 150:300]
    print("crop shares memory with the image:", np.shares_memory(crop, f), " after .copy():", np.shares_memory(crop.copy(), f))
our matrix matches cv2.getRotationMatrix2D: True forward mapping: 13.5% of covered output pixels are holes inverse bilinear vs cv2.warpAffine: max diff 1.4e-02 nearest after 12 x 30 deg: PSNR 28.65 dB bilinear after 12 x 30 deg: PSNR 26.56 dB bicubic after 12 x 30 deg: PSNR 31.67 dB Lanczos-4 after 12 x 30 deg: PSNR 35.65 dB nearest (decimate) contrast beyond new Nyquist (std): 0.354 INTER_AREA contrast beyond new Nyquist (std): 0.039 Gaussian then decimate contrast beyond new Nyquist (std): 0.001 H @ H_inv ~ I (scaled): True rectified page: mean abs error 3.90 grey levels crop shares memory with the image: True after .copy(): False

Our bilinear inverse warp agrees with OpenCV to within 0.014 (on a [0, 1] scale): OpenCV computes interpolation weights in fixed point, quantising the fractional offsets to 1/32 of a pixel, a speed/accuracy trade-off worth knowing when comparing implementations. The accumulated-error test rotates the image twelve times by 30° and compares with the original inside a central disc. Every resampling step low-pass filters the image a little, and the errors compound: bilinear is worst (26.6 dB) and Lanczos best (35.7 dB). Nearest neighbour (28.7 dB) beats bilinear here because it never blurs, it only displaces pixels by up to half a pixel each time; its jagged edges are clearly visible, though (Figure 21). The practical rule: compose all transforms into one matrix and resample once.

8.4 Scaling and aliasing

Enlarging an image asks the interpolator to invent values between samples; shrinking it discards samples, and the sampling theorem says what happens to detail finer than the new grid can represent: it does not disappear but folds back as false, lower-frequency patterns (aliasing) [30]. The cure is to low-pass filter before decimating. The zone plate test makes this visible: its local frequency rises with radius, so naive 4× decimation creates spurious rings far from the centre (standard deviation 0.354 in the region beyond the new Nyquist limit), whereas cv2.INTER_AREA (pixel-area averaging, OpenCV's recommended method for shrinking) leaves 0.039 and a Gaussian pre-blur of σ = 1.6 leaves 0.001 (Figure 22). The same reasoning explains §2's stride-2 checkerboard and why §9's pyramid blurs before every subsampling step. Libraries differ in whether they anti-alias by default (scikit-image's resize does when downsampling; OpenCV's resize with INTER_LINEAR does not), so resizing the same image in a training pipeline and in production with different libraries can change a model's input noticeably.

8.5 Perspective warping

The last part simulates a page photographed at an angle by warping it with a homography, then rectifies it with the homography computed from the four corner correspondences by cv2.getPerspectiveTransform. The round trip leaves a mean absolute error of 3.9 grey levels, the cost of two cubic resamplings of sharp text. In practice the corners are detected rather than known; §10 does that with thresholding, morphology and contour approximation. Geometric transforms also underpin data augmentation for training vision models, where random crops, flips, rotations and scalings are applied to every training image [62].

Crop = slice In NumPy, img[100:200, 150:300] is a view sharing memory with img: writing into the crop writes into the original. Call .copy() when the crop must be independent, as the last output line shows.
Exercises · §8
  1. Write the 2 × 3 matrix that OpenCV returns for a 90° rotation about (255.5, 255.5) with scale 1, using its form with rows (α, β, (1 − α)cx − βcy) and (−β, α, βcx + (1 − α)cy), where α = s cos θ, β = s sin θ. Where does the input pixel (511, 0) go?
    Show solution

    α = 0 and β = 1. Row 1: (0, 1, 1·255.5 − 1·255.5) = (0, 1, 0). Row 2: (−1, 0, 255.5 + 255.5) = (−1, 0, 511). Then (x, y) = (511, 0) maps to (0·511 + 1·0 + 0, −511 + 0 + 511) = (0, 0): the top-right corner goes to the top-left, which is a 90° counter-clockwise rotation as displayed.

  2. Bilinearly interpolate f at (x, y) = (1.3, 2.6) given f(1, 2) = 10, f(2, 2) = 20, f(1, 3) = 30 and f(2, 3) = 40 (written as f(x, y)).
    Show solution

    a = 0.3, b = 0.6. Weights: (1 − a)(1 − b) = 0.28 for (1, 2), a(1 − b) = 0.12 for (2, 2), (1 − a)b = 0.42 for (1, 3), ab = 0.18 for (2, 3). Value = 2.8 + 2.4 + 12.6 + 7.2 = 25.0. Because these four values form a plane (f = 10x + 20y − 40), bilinear interpolation reproduces it exactly: 13 + 52 − 40 = 25.

  3. Why is nearest-neighbour interpolation mandatory when warping a segmentation label map, and what goes wrong with bilinear?
    Show solution

    Labels are categories, not quantities: averaging label 1 (road) and label 3 (car) gives 2 (perhaps "person"), a class that is not present. Bilinear or bicubic interpolation creates such invalid labels along every boundary. Nearest neighbour only copies existing labels. (An alternative for soft masks is to warp one-hot channels bilinearly and take the argmax.)

  4. How many point correspondences determine an affine transform, and how many a homography? Why does getPerspectiveTransform need exactly four points while findHomography accepts more?
    Show solution

    Each correspondence gives two equations. Affine has 6 unknowns, so 3 non-collinear points; a homography has 8 (9 entries up to scale), so 4 points with no three collinear. getPerspectiveTransform solves the exactly determined 8 × 8 linear system. findHomography solves an over-determined least-squares problem (and optionally RANSAC) from many, possibly noisy or wrong, matches, which is the normal situation with detected features [56].

  5. You downscale a 4000-pixel-wide photo to 500 pixels for a CNN. Estimate a suitable Gaussian pre-filter σ and explain the risk of using cv2.resize(..., interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR) directly.
    Show solution

    The factor is 8. The new Nyquist frequency is 1/16 cycle per original pixel; a common rule of thumb is σ ≈ 0.5 × factor to (factor − 1)/2, i.e. about 3.5–4 pixels (scikit-image's default is (factor − 1)/2 = 3.5). INTER_LINEAR samples a 2 × 2 neighbourhood at each output position, ignoring 60 of every 64 input pixels, so fine textures (fabric, brick, foliage, text) alias into moiré and the result changes with sub-pixel shifts of the input. INTER_AREA or an explicit blur avoids this.

§9Image pyramids and multiscale analysis

Objects appear at unknown sizes, and image structure exists at every scale, from texture grain to whole-object shape. Multiscale representations make scale explicit. The continuous ideal is scale space: the family of images L(·, σ) = Gσ ∗ f for all σ ≥ 0, in which, for the Gaussian kernel and under natural axioms, no new structure is created as σ grows [18,63]. A pyramid is its economical discrete version: blur, then subsample by 2, and repeat [64].

9.1 Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids

The Gaussian pyramid is a sequence of low-pass images, each half the size of the previous one. Burt and Adelson's generating kernel w is a 5-tap separable filter whose weights [1/4 − a/2, 1/4, a, 1/4, 1/4 − a/2] satisfy normalisation, symmetry and "equal contribution" (every input pixel contributes the same total weight to the next level); a = 0.375 gives [1 4 6 4 1]/16, a close binomial approximation of a Gaussian [64]. Because each level has a quarter of the pixels of the previous one, the whole pyramid costs at most 1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + … = 4/3 of the original image.

The Laplacian pyramid stores the differences between each Gaussian level and the upsampled next level. Each band contains the detail at one octave of scale and is close to zero in flat regions, so it is sparse and compresses well; that was its original purpose as "a compact image code" [64]. Its name comes from the fact that a difference of Gaussians approximates the Laplacian of a Gaussian, the same band-pass operator SIFT searches for keypoints across scales [65]. Reconstruction runs the construction backwards and is exact for any choice of filter, because each band was defined as precisely what the coarser level fails to predict.

pyramids.pyREDUCE/EXPAND, exact reconstruction, coefficient sparsity, multiband blending ran

"""Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids, exact reconstruction, and multiband blending."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from skimage import data, util, transform, metrics

# Burt & Adelson's 5-tap generating kernel with a = 0.375: [1 4 6 4 1] / 16
W5 = np.array([1, 4, 6, 4, 1], np.float64) / 16


def reduce_(img):
    """Blur with the separable 5x5 kernel, then keep every second row and column."""
    b = cv2.sepFilter2D(img, -1, W5, W5, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
    return b[::2, ::2]


def expand(img, shape):
    """Upsample by inserting zeros, then blur with 4x the kernel (to restore the mean)."""
    up = np.zeros(shape[:2] + img.shape[2:], img.dtype)
    up[::2, ::2] = img
    return cv2.sepFilter2D(up, -1, 2 * W5, 2 * W5, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)


def gaussian_pyramid(img, levels):
    G = [img]
    for _ in range(levels - 1):
        G.append(reduce_(G[-1]))
    return G


def laplacian_pyramid(img, levels):
    G = gaussian_pyramid(img, levels)
    return [G[i] - expand(G[i + 1], G[i].shape) for i in range(levels - 1)] + [G[-1]]


def collapse(L):
    x = L[-1]
    for band in reversed(L[:-1]):
        x = band + expand(x, band.shape)
    return x


def blend(a, b, mask, levels=6):
    """Multiband blending: combine Laplacian bands of a and b with a Gaussian pyramid of the mask."""
    La, Lb = laplacian_pyramid(a, levels), laplacian_pyramid(b, levels)
    Gm = gaussian_pyramid(mask, levels)
    return collapse([m * x + (1 - m) * y for x, y, m in zip(La, Lb, Gm)])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    f = util.img_as_float(data.camera())
    G = gaussian_pyramid(f, 5)
    print("Gaussian pyramid shapes:", [g.shape for g in G])
    ocv = cv2.pyrDown(f)
    print(f"reduce_ vs cv2.pyrDown: max diff {np.abs(G[1] - ocv).max():.1e}")
    print(f"total pixels / original: {sum(g.size for g in G) / f.size:.3f}  (limit 4/3 = 1.333)")

    L = laplacian_pyramid(f, 5)
    print(f"collapse(laplacian) == original: max err {np.abs(collapse(L) - f).max():.1e}")
    for i, band in enumerate(L[:-1]):
        print(f"  L{i} {str(band.shape):10s} mean {band.mean():+.4f}  std {band.std():.4f}  |x|<0.02: {np.mean(np.abs(band) < 0.02):.2f}")

    # compression intuition: quantise the band-pass levels coarsely
    Lq = [np.round(b / 0.04) * 0.04 for b in L[:-1]] + [L[-1]]
    nz = sum(np.count_nonzero(np.round(b / 0.04)) for b in L[:-1])
    print(f"quantised bands (step 0.04): {nz / f.size:.2%} non-zero coefficients, "
          f"PSNR {metrics.peak_signal_noise_ratio(f, np.clip(collapse(Lq), 0, 1), data_range=1):.2f} dB")

    # blending two images along a vertical seam
    a = transform.resize(util.img_as_float(data.chelsea()), (256, 256), anti_aliasing=True)
    b = transform.resize(util.img_as_float(data.coffee()), (256, 256), anti_aliasing=True)
    mask = np.zeros((256, 256, 3)); mask[:, :128] = 1
    hard = mask * a + (1 - mask) * b
    feathered = {}
    for fs in (2, 16):
        m = cv2.GaussianBlur(mask, (0, 0), fs)
        feathered[fs] = m * a + (1 - m) * b
    multi = np.clip(blend(a, b, mask), 0, 1)
    def seam_jump(x):   # largest column-to-column change of the column-mean colour near the seam
        prof = cv2.GaussianBlur(x, (0, 0), 3).mean(axis=0)            # (256, 3) coarse profile
        return np.abs(np.diff(prof[96:160], axis=0)).sum(-1).max()
    def detail_kept(x, src, cols):   # correlation of fine detail (x - blur) with the source's
        hp = lambda y: (y - cv2.GaussianBlur(y, (0, 0), 1.5))[:, cols].ravel()
        return np.corrcoef(hp(x), hp(src))[0, 1]
    near_a, near_b = slice(108, 124), slice(132, 148)               # 4 to 20 px either side of the seam
    print(f"{'':16s} {'coarse seam step':>16s} {'cat detail kept':>16s} {'coffee detail kept':>19s}")
    for name, x in [("hard cut", hard), ("feathered s=2", feathered[2]), ("feathered s=16", feathered[16]),
                    ("Laplacian blend", multi)]:
        print(f"{name:16s} {seam_jump(x):16.4f} {detail_kept(x, a, near_a):16.3f} {detail_kept(x, b, near_b):19.3f}")
    np.save("_blend.npy", np.stack([a, b, hard, feathered[2], feathered[16], multi]))
Gaussian pyramid shapes: [(512, 512), (256, 256), (128, 128), (64, 64), (32, 32)] reduce_ vs cv2.pyrDown: max diff 3.3e-16 total pixels / original: 1.332 (limit 4/3 = 1.333) collapse(laplacian) == original: max err 6.9e-17 L0 (512, 512) mean -0.0000 std 0.0420 |x|<0.02: 0.70 L1 (256, 256) mean +0.0000 std 0.0389 |x|<0.02: 0.76 L2 (128, 128) mean +0.0000 std 0.0410 |x|<0.02: 0.74 L3 (64, 64) mean +0.0001 std 0.0464 |x|<0.02: 0.69 quantised bands (step 0.04): 37.99% non-zero coefficients, PSNR 37.64 dB coarse seam step cat detail kept coffee detail kept hard cut 0.0290 1.000 1.000 feathered s=2 0.0289 0.999 0.999 feathered s=16 0.0187 0.953 0.977 Laplacian blend 0.0251 1.000 1.000

Our reduce_ matches cv2.pyrDown to 3 × 10⁻¹⁶ (OpenCV uses the same 5-tap kernel), the five-level pyramid uses 1.332 times the original pixel count, and collapsing the Laplacian pyramid reproduces the image to 7 × 10⁻¹⁷. The band statistics show the sparsity: each band has mean zero and 69–76% of its coefficients are smaller than 0.02 in magnitude. Quantising the bands with a step of 0.04 leaves only 38% non-zero coefficients and still reconstructs at 37.6 dB, which is the essence of transform coding (Figure 24).

9.2 Multiband blending

Joining two images along a seam shows the value of separating scales. A hard cut leaves a visible step wherever the colours differ; a narrow feather keeps the step; a wide feather hides the step but superimposes the two images' fine detail over a wide band ("ghosting"). Burt and Adelson's multiresolution spline blends each Laplacian band separately, using a mask taken from the Gaussian pyramid of the seam, so that coarse structure transitions over a wide zone and fine detail over a narrow one [66]. The output measures both properties near the seam: the coarse step (largest change of the column-mean colour after a σ = 3 blur) and how well each side's fine detail survives within 4–20 pixels of the seam. A wide feather (σ = 16) gives the smallest step but keeps only 95–98% of the detail correlation; the Laplacian blend reduces the step relative to the hard cut while keeping fine detail intact (correlation 1.000) (Figure 25). Panorama stitchers use multiband blending for exactly this reason.

9.3 Beyond Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids

The Laplacian pyramid is overcomplete (4/3 coefficients per pixel) and not oriented. The wavelet transform gives a critically sampled multiresolution decomposition with horizontal, vertical and diagonal detail bands [67] (it is what denoise_wavelet in §6 shrinks), and the steerable pyramid splits each scale into several orientations while remaining shift- and rotation-friendly [68]. Deep networks rebuilt the same idea from learned features: feature pyramid networks combine a coarse-to-fine top-down path with lateral connections to detect objects at every scale [69].

Exercises · §9
  1. Show that a Gaussian pyramid on an N × N image never needs more than 4N²/3 values. How many values does the 5-level pyramid of the 512 × 512 camera image hold?
    Show solution

    Level k has N²/4k values; the geometric series sums to N²/(1 − 1/4) = 4N²/3 for infinitely many levels. For five levels: 512² + 256² + 128² + 64² + 32² = 262,144 + 65,536 + 16,384 + 4,096 + 1,024 = 349,184 = 1.332 × 262,144, as printed.

  2. Prove that collapsing a Laplacian pyramid reconstructs the image exactly, whatever filter REDUCE and EXPAND use.
    Show solution

    By definition Lk = Gk − EXPAND(Gk+1) and Ltop = Gtop. Collapsing starts with x = Ltop = Gtop and computes Lk + EXPAND(x). If x = Gk+1, this equals Gk exactly; by induction the final result is G₀ = f. No property of the filter is used, only the fact that the same EXPAND is applied in both directions. (Quantising the bands breaks the exactness, which is where filter quality matters.)

  3. Verify that a = 0.375 in Burt and Adelson's kernel [1/4 − a/2, 1/4, a, 1/4, 1/4 − a/2] gives [1 4 6 4 1]/16, and check the equal-contribution property.
    Show solution

    1/4 − 0.1875 = 0.0625 = 1/16, 1/4 = 4/16, 0.375 = 6/16. Equal contribution: after subsampling by 2, each input sample is weighted either by the even taps (1/16 + 6/16 + 1/16 = 1/2) or by the odd taps (4/16 + 4/16 = 1/2), so every input pixel contributes 1/2 per axis to the next level. The weights sum to 1, so mean brightness is preserved.

  4. Why does EXPAND multiply the kernel by 4 (2 per axis)?
    Show solution

    Inserting zeros between samples (↑2) leaves only one in four values non-zero in 2-D, so the mean drops by a factor of 4. Interpolating with w (sum 1) would preserve that reduced mean. Multiplying by 4 restores it: in 1-D, each output sample receives weights from either the odd taps or the even taps of 2w, both of which sum to 1.

  5. For blending two 512 × 512 images, how many pyramid levels would you use, and what goes wrong with too few or too many?
    Show solution

    The coarsest level's mask transition is about 2levels−1 pixels wide at full resolution, so it should match the scale of the largest colour or brightness difference to be hidden; for whole-image exposure differences, 6–8 levels (coarsest 16 × 16 to 4 × 4) are typical. Too few levels give a transition that is too narrow, so a low-frequency step remains visible (like the narrow feather). Too many levels average the two images' overall colour across the whole frame, so one side's tint bleeds far into the other.

§10Capstone: cleaning up a photographed page

Real tasks chain several operations, and the order matters. The capstone builds a miniature document-scanning pipeline from the tools of the previous sections. A synthetic page with known ink (so the result can be scored exactly) is "photographed": placed on a dark desk, tilted by a homography, darkened by a soft diagonal shadow, slightly blurred and corrupted with sensor noise. The pipeline then has to find the page, undo the perspective, remove the shading and binarise the text (Figure 26).

pipeline.pysimulated phone photo of a page and a five-step clean-up ran

"""Capstone: clean up a phone photo of a page with operations from every section."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
from skimage import filters


def make_page(w=480, h=320):
    """A clean synthetic page with known ink: the ground truth for scoring."""
    page = np.full((h, w), 235, np.uint8)
    lines = ["Image processing transforms images", "to improve their quality or to make",
             "later analysis easier. Point ops,", "filters, transforms, morphology and",
             "geometric warps are its building", "blocks. 0123456789 (x, y) -> (u, v)"]
    for i, t in enumerate(lines):
        cv2.putText(page, t, (18, 42 + 48 * i), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 0.78, 30, 2, cv2.LINE_AA)
    return page, page < 128


def simulate_photo(page, rng):
    """Paste the page on a dark desk, tilt it, light it unevenly, blur and add sensor noise."""
    h, w = page.shape
    canvas = np.full((h + 120, w + 120), 20, np.float32)
    src = np.float32([[0, 0], [w, 0], [w, h], [0, h]])
    dst = np.float32([[90, 70], [w + 70, 40], [w + 20, h + 95], [45, h + 70]])
    Hm = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(src, dst)
    warped = cv2.warpPerspective(page.astype(np.float32), Hm, canvas.shape[::-1], flags=cv2.INTER_CUBIC,
                                 borderValue=-1)
    shot = np.where(warped >= 0, warped, canvas)
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:shot.shape[0], :shot.shape[1]]
    shadow = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(xx + 0.6 * yy - 0.55 * xx.max()) / 25))           # a soft diagonal shadow
    shot *= (0.3 + 0.7 * shadow) * (0.85 + 0.15 * xx / xx.max())
    shot = cv2.GaussianBlur(shot, (0, 0), 0.8) + rng.normal(0, 6, shot.shape)
    return np.clip(shot, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8), dst


def order_corners(pts):
    """Return corners as top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left."""
    s, d = pts.sum(1), np.diff(pts, axis=1).ravel()
    return np.float32([pts[s.argmin()], pts[d.argmin()], pts[s.argmax()], pts[d.argmax()]])


def find_page(shot):
    """Log + Otsu threshold, morphology, contour approximation -> the page's four corners."""
    logim = np.log1p(cv2.GaussianBlur(shot, (0, 0), 3).astype(np.float32))   # shading becomes additive
    bw = logim > filters.threshold_otsu(logim)
    bw = cv2.morphologyEx(bw.astype(np.uint8), cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, np.ones((15, 15), np.uint8))  # close the text
    cnts, _ = cv2.findContours(bw, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
    c = max(cnts, key=cv2.contourArea)
    quad = cv2.approxPolyDP(c, 0.02 * cv2.arcLength(c, True), True).reshape(-1, 2)
    assert len(quad) == 4, f"expected 4 corners, got {len(quad)}"
    return order_corners(quad.astype(np.float32))


def clean_page(shot, size):
    w, h = size
    corners = find_page(shot)
    Hinv = cv2.getPerspectiveTransform(corners, np.float32([[0, 0], [w, 0], [w, h], [0, h]]))
    rect = cv2.warpPerspective(shot, Hinv, (w, h), flags=cv2.INTER_CUBIC)                  # §8
    den = cv2.medianBlur(rect, 3)                                                         # §3
    bg = cv2.morphologyEx(den, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE, (21, 21)))  # §5
    flat = np.clip(den.astype(np.float32) / np.maximum(bg, 1) * 255, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)  # §1: divide out
    ink = flat < filters.threshold_sauvola(flat, window_size=25, k=0.2)                    # §1
    return corners, rect, flat, ink


def f_measure(pred, ref):
    tp = (pred & ref).sum()
    return 2 * tp / (pred.sum() + ref.sum())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
    page, ref = make_page()
    shot, true_corners = simulate_photo(page, rng)
    corners, rect, flat, ink = clean_page(shot, page.shape[::-1])
    print("corner error (px):", np.round(np.linalg.norm(corners - true_corners, axis=1), 1))
    naive = rect < filters.threshold_otsu(rect)
    print(f"ink F-measure vs ground truth:\n  Otsu on rectified        {f_measure(naive, ref):.3f}\n"
          f"  Otsu after flattening    {f_measure(flat < filters.threshold_otsu(flat), ref):.3f}\n"
          f"  full pipeline (Sauvola)  {f_measure(ink, ref):.3f}")
    print(f"illumination ratio right/left before {rect[:, -40:].mean() / rect[:, :40].mean():.2f}, "
          f"after {flat[:, -40:].mean() / flat[:, :40].mean():.2f}")
    np.save("_pipe.npy", np.array([shot, rect, flat, ink, naive], dtype=object), allow_pickle=True)
corner error (px): [2.8 1.4 1. 2.8] ink F-measure vs ground truth: Otsu on rectified 0.369 Otsu after flattening 0.777 full pipeline (Sauvola) 0.769 illumination ratio right/left before 3.65, after 1.11

Three design decisions carry the result:

  • Thresholding in the log domain to find the page. Shading multiplies brightness, so in a plain Otsu threshold the shadowed half of the page falls into the "desk" class, and in a first version of this code the detected corners were off by over 100 pixels. Taking the logarithm turns the multiplicative shadow into an additive offset that is small compared with the page–desk contrast, and Otsu then separates page from desk; the corners are found to within 3 pixels.
  • Dividing, not subtracting, the background. Under the image formation model observed = illumination × reflectance, dividing by a background estimate recovers reflectance, so ink has the same contrast in the shadow as in the light. The closing with a 21-pixel disk erases the strokes and leaves the illumination; after division the right/left brightness ratio falls from 3.65 to 1.11.
  • Order of operations. Rectifying first makes the text upright and of uniform size, so the square structuring element and the Sauvola window mean the same thing everywhere on the page.

The score is the F-measure of the ink pixels against the known ground truth. Global Otsu on the rectified image reaches only 0.37 because the whole shadowed region is labelled ink (Figure 27). After flattening, both global Otsu (0.78) and Sauvola (0.77) work; once the illumination has been removed the local threshold has little left to correct. The remaining errors are mostly stroke-width differences from the blur, noise and two resamplings, not misplaced text.

Exercises · §10
  1. Swap steps 2 and 4: estimate and divide out the background on the tilted photo first, then rectify. What changes, and which order do you expect to work better?
    Show solution

    In the unrectified photo the text is foreshortened: strokes are thinner on the far edge of the page, and the desk is in the frame. The closing would have to handle the desk–page boundary (where it would spread the bright page over the desk) and a structuring element sized for the near edge would be too large for the far edge. Flattening after rectification sees only the page at uniform scale, so it is the more robust order; flattening first can work if the background estimate is restricted to the page mask.

  2. Replace the morphological closing in clean_page with a large median filter (for example 31 × 31) as the background estimator. When would each be preferable?
    Show solution

    A median of a window in which text covers less than half of the pixels returns a paper value, so it also removes text, and it is less sensitive than a closing to isolated bright noise (a closing propagates the maximum of each window, so a single hot pixel enlarges into a bright blob in the background estimate). The closing is better when text is dense (more than half of some windows is ink, where the median would return ink), as long as the structuring element is wider than the strokes. Both are cheap with O(1)-per-pixel algorithms [21,35].

  3. The pipeline assumes that the page is the largest bright region and that approxPolyDP returns exactly four vertices. Describe two failure cases and a fix for each.
    Show solution

    (a) A bright object on the desk (a white mug) is larger than the page or touches it, so the largest contour is wrong or merged: restrict candidates to convex quadrilaterals with plausible aspect ratio and area, or separate touching objects with an opening before finding contours. (b) A curled corner or a finger over the edge gives 5–6 vertices or a rounded corner: increase the approximation tolerance progressively until four vertices remain, or fit four lines to the contour (e.g. with a Hough transform) and intersect them. The assertion in find_page exists so that such cases fail loudly instead of producing a garbage warp.

Part of a series on computer vision. Companion articles cover core vision tasks, deep learning for vision, camera models and 3-D geometry, video understanding and tracking, generative and vision-language models, production engineering, evaluation and reliability, and application domains. All code blocks marked “ran” were executed with the library versions listed in the introduction; outputs are reproduced verbatim.
